It writes a registry to `project/.cache/e2e-real/` so created resources can be audited later. Run `openyida login` for the target environment before starting the real E2E runner. `test:e2e:real:full` extends the smoke path into a broad deterministic feature matrix: auth/env, app update, form update and option mutation, page build/compile/generate/publish, data create/get/update/query, permission read, page config and short URL check, report create/append, dashboard skill verification, export/import, batch, task-center, formula/doctor/sample/CDN config, and local connector parsing/template generation. AI-backed commands such as `flash-to-prd` are available as the optional `ai` stage because they depend on remote model availability. Workflow mutation is available as the opt-in `process` stage; it creates and republishes a workflow on the disposable E2E form and records advanced official-node fixtures for review. `test:e2e:real:skills` enforces coverage for every directory under `yida-skills/skills/`. Each skill must be classified as real E2E, offline/unit, opt-in, or deprecated with an explicit reason. This prevents new skills from quietly bypassing the real-environment test plan. Each successful full run leaves a human-inspectable result app in the target organization. The final step publishes a dedicated `Full E2E Dashboard` custom page, renames the app to `OY_E2E_*_PASSED` by default, and prints direct links for the app, form, dashboard page, and report; the same links are saved under `resultApp` in the registry JSON. Useful options: | Env var | Purpose | |---------|---------| | `OPENYIDA_E2E_PREFIX` | Override the disposable resource name prefix | | `OPENYIDA_E2E_CORP_ID` | Switch to the dedicated test organization before creating resources | | `OPENYIDA_E2E_RESULT_APP_NAME` | Override the final app name shown as the full-run result | | `OPENYIDA_E2E_BASE_URL` | Override the Yida base URL for private deployments | | `OPENYIDA_E2E_FIELDS_FILE` | Use a custom form fields fixture | | `OPENYIDA_E2E_PAGE_SOURCE` | Use a custom page source for publish verification | | `OPENYIDA_E2E_SKIP_PUBLISH=1` | Skip custom page creation and publish | | `OPENYIDA_E2E_REGISTRY_DIR` | Write registries outside `project/.cache/e2e-real/` | | `OPENYIDA_E2E_FULL_STAGES` | Comma-separated stage list for `test:e2e:real:full`; use `all` or omit for the default broad matrix | Use `npm run test:e2e:real:cleanup` to list recorded disposable resources. OpenYida does not yet expose a safe app/form deletion command, so cleanup is intentionally a registry-backed audit step rather than an automatic destructive action. ### Skill Evaluation Harness The E2E paths above prove the *CLI* works. The eval harness under `scripts/eval/` measures whether the *agent* still routes natural-language requests to the right sub-skill and produces good output after you edit `yida-skills/SKILL.md`. It is the feedback loop for harness engineering. ```bash # Routing eval — "did it pick the right sub-skill?" No real resources, no login. # Drives a headless `claude -p` agent with each scenario prompt and checks # the selected sub-skill against the golden set. npm run eval:routing # Doc quality — static analysis of all SKILL.md files (standards + maintainability). npm run eval:doc-quality # Safety — credential leak detection, command whitelist, corpId consistency. npm run eval:safety # Coverage — how much of the skill/category/reference space is covered by scenarios. npm run eval:coverage # Comprehensive — 10-dimension scorecard for a single skill (doc quality, routing, # safety, step completeness, output validity, efficiency, stability, coverage). # Outputs a JSON scorecard, SVG radar chart, and trend analysis. npm run eval:comprehensive -- --skill yida-dashboard # Tool-pipeline baseline (end-to-end) — wraps the real-environment runner for one # sub-skill, adds guardrail assertions, screenshots the published page, and writes a # human scoring template. Runs deterministic CLI commands (no agent) so it serves as # a control that proves the build→publish→screenshot→score plumbing itself works. # Requires OPENYIDA_E2E=1 and a valid token session. OPENYIDA_E2E=1 npm run eval:e2e -- --skill yida-dashboard --screenshot # Same, plus automatic screenshot scoring via the local multimodal `claude -p`. OPENYIDA_E2E=1 npm run eval:e2e -- --skill yida-dashboard --screenshot --auto-score # Real-generation eval — "can one sentence really build a usable app?" Feeds a # natural-language request ("帮我创建一个订单管理系统") to a headless `claude -p` # that actually reads the openyida skill and runs the CLI to build a real app, then # reuses the screenshot + scoring + report pipeline. Creates real 宜搭 resources, so # it needs OPENYIDA_E2E=1 + an authenticated agent. Unlike the deterministic baseline # above, here the agent self-orchestrates. OPENYIDA_E2E=1 npm run eval:generate -- --screenshot # Re-evaluate an archived real CLI trace against the latest scenario contract and # current read-only platform state. This does not run an agent or mutate resources. npm run eval:replay -- --report --scenario --app-type APP_XXX # Run all three in one pass (routing + tool-pipeline baseline + real generation). OPENYIDA_E2E=1 npm run eval:all -- --skill yida-dashboard --screenshot # Optional: a zero-dependency local web console (buttons + live streamed output) # that runs the tasks above on click. Binds to 127.0.0.1 only; tasks are a fixed # whitelist. Use the Node version you start it with, so run `nvm use 20` first. npm run eval:dashboard # http://127.0.0.1:4500 ``` Configuration precedence is `CLI flag > env (OPENYIDA_EVAL_*) > scripts/eval/eval.config.json > defaults`. | Flag | Purpose | |------|---------| | `--mode e2e\|routing\|generate\|doc-quality\|safety\|coverage\|comprehensive\|all` | Which evals to run (default `e2e`) | | `--skill ` | Restrict the e2e run to one sub-skill; stages are reverse-looked-up from the `SKILL_COVERAGE` matrix | | `--stages a,b` | Explicit stage list, overriding the skill reverse-lookup | | `--runs N` | Multi-run stability: repeat routing N times, report consistency rate | | `--screenshot` / `--no-screenshot` | Capture the published page (default on; skipped gracefully if Playwright is absent) | | `--auto-score` / `--no-auto-score` | Score screenshots with the local `claude -p` agent (default off → human template only) | | `--scenarios ` | Routing golden-set directory (default `scripts/eval/scenarios`) | | `--gen-scenarios ` | Real-generation golden-set directory (default `scripts/eval/scenarios/generation`) | Results are written back into the existing `acceptance-manifest.json` under a new `eval` section (guardrails, screenshots, scores) plus two sibling artifacts: a `scoring.md` human-scoring template and a self-contained `eval-report.html` visual report (screenshots inlined as base64, so the single file opens anywhere). Routing results land in `project/.cache/eval/routing-report.json`; generation results (with their own `scoring.md` + `eval-report.html`) land in `project/.cache/eval/generate/gen-/`. The harness degrades gracefully: a missing Playwright skips screenshots (enable with `npm install --no-save playwright && npx playwright install chromium`), and a missing `claude` CLI skips auto-scoring while keeping the human template. A guardrail failure (for example a resource-creating command issued before a successful `login --check-only`) fails the run. A zero-dependency local dashboard (`npm run eval:dashboard`, then open `http://127.0.0.1:4500`) drives these runs from buttons and streams output live; its "📊 查看最新报告" button opens the most recent `eval-report.html`. ### Connectors, Integrations, and Reports Automation spec `sendMessage` nodes accept `toRoles: [{"roleCode":"REAL_ROLE_ID","roleName":"Finance"}]` for NORMAL messages, alongside users and member fields. Process approval, operator, and CC nodes can also select roles. Role selection differs from conditional actor selection, which does not yet have a complete CLI shorthand. See the `yida-flow-node-config` skill for shared node guidance. ```bash openyida connector smart-create --curl "curl https://api.example.com/users" openyida connector list openyida integration create APP_XXX FORM_XXX "Sync customer data" openyida integration create APP_XXX FORM_XXX "Approval result notify" \ --events processFinish --approval-actions agree,disagree --receivers 123456 # Capability probe only; currently fails closed before auth/spec reads/remote writes openyida integration update APP_XXX FORM_XXX LPROC_XXX \ --spec .cache/openyida/integration/desired-spec.json openyida create-report APP_XXX "Sales Dashboard" .cache/openyida/reports/charts.json openyida append-chart APP_XXX REPORT_XXX .cache/openyida/reports/chart.json # Aggregate tables use two independent optimistic-concurrency axes. openyida aggregate-table inspect APP_XXX FORM_XXX --json openyida aggregate-table preview APP_XXX FORM_XXX .cache/openyida/aggregate/design.json --json openyida aggregate-table save APP_XXX FORM_XXX .cache/openyida/aggregate/design.json --json --no-open openyida aggregate-table publish APP_XXX FORM_XXX .cache/openyida/aggregate/design.json --json --no-open openyida aggregate-table status APP_XXX FORM_XXX --json ``` Aggregate-table `save` verifies the draft `stashGmtModified` axis; `publish` verifies the live `gmtModified` axis. Both commands require the corresponding GET readback revision to advance; when a response revision exists it must equal that readback axis. Both commands also require canonical readback of `relationForms`, `relationships`, `aggregatedFields`, `auxFields`, `formulaFields`, and `validators`. The CLI intentionally does not expose aggregate-table deletion, AI authoring, a high-level design DSL, or tenant-dynamic limits until the corresponding platform contracts are proven. The opt-in aggregate real-E2E runner additionally requires `OPENYIDA_AGGREGATE_E2E_RUN_ID` and an exact `OPENYIDA_AGGREGATE_E2E_OWNED_MARKER` beginning with `__`. Before its first write it verifies the exact list/inspect identity and name, persists a redacted manifest, registry, and baseline snapshot, then conditionally restores the baseline using the latest live revision. Missing ownership proof or concurrent revision movement produces `PLATFORM_PROBE_REQUIRED` / `restore_blocked` without a restore write. ## CLI Reference Run `openyida --help` or `openyida --help` for detailed usage. ### Report a problem or contribute a fix Tell your AI: “OpenYida keeps failing. <appType> --type todo --normalized`; `created`, `done`, and `cc` select the other personal task lists. Use `openyida task-center capabilities --json` for supported filters and the page configuration example. The default `app-v1` transport preserves the existing queries. Select `--transport app-query` for additional server filters while keeping the query fixed to the target application: `--originators '["USER_ID"]'` accepts one originator, `--process-codes '["PROCESS_CODE"]'` selects processes, and date bounds use Unix milliseconds. Available fields vary by task kind; unsupported fields fail before a request. `openyida task-center options <appType> --type originators|processes|forms --keyword TEXT --json` returns readable lookup options. The CLI never silently falls back to an unfiltered query. After explicitly choosing a custom task page, run `openyida task-center scaffold --spec <file.json> --output <new-file.canvas.jsx>`. The configuration requires the choice record and the application's existing design file. Generated pages follow the application theme, read the current visitor's tasks, and open native pages for processing. `embedded` mode provides the same task section for an existing workbench. Compile and publish the page using the usual commands. Page configurations can explicitly set `transport: "app-query"` and per-kind initial filters, for example `filters: { "todo": { "originators": ["USER_ID"] } }`. Generated pages include the same `filterSchema`, `normalizeFilters`, task loader, and option lookup helpers as the CLI. Use `task-center count <appType> --type todo --transport app-query --filters-json '{"keyword":"purchase"}' --json` for a one-record query with a matching server total; an unknown total remains `null`. `task-center inspect <appType> --process-inst-id <id> [--form-uuid <id>] [--history] [--task-id <id>] --json` reads an authorized linked process and optional operation history. Personal task outcomes, selected-task outcomes and final process results remain separate. Read commands do not create custom pages or require a custom-page choice. Scaffolds select only the needed task kinds, `fields` and `filterFields`; the default is a single todo list. `view: "progress", mode: "embedded"` provides a progress component for an existing business page, using its real linked `processInstanceId`. History and task-row expansion are opt-in. See the [workflow capability reference](yida-skills/skills/yida-canvas-data-binding/references/workflow-capabilities.md) for configuration and integration examples. ### CLI Notes #### Connector Safety and Real E2E `connector test` keeps the legacy flat `--params` option, but dispatches each key only to the location proven by the action schema. Unknown or ambiguous keys fail closed. Authenticated connectors require `--account-id`, and that account must belong to the selected connector. The test response follows the frontend canonical contract `{statusLine,responseHeaders,content}`; unknown envelopes and non-2xx status lines are failures. With `--ignore-defaults`, the test starts from empty parameter sets: saved default values from the action definition (including sensitive placeholder values such as documented `***` samples) are ignored for the run, and a warning is printed when a non-empty systemToken default exists. Declared systemToken actions still require `--system-token-app`, target-trust checks still apply, and explicitly provided systemToken values are still rejected. `connector update-action --connector-id <id> --action <operationId> --query-json '{"currentPage":"1"}' --confirm` is the narrow safe path for editing existing query defaults. It requires a complete connector/action preflight, changes only declared query defaults mirrored in `inputs` and `parameters`, submits the complete action collection once, and verifies an unchanged connector fingerprint, action count, non-target actions, and stable IDs. Missing/empty/unknown parameters, duplicate IDs, incomplete readback, and unknown write outcomes fail closed without automatic retry. `add-action` no longer overwrites an existing action ID; use `update-action` for query-only edits. The opt-in connector E2E is intentionally separate from the shared full runner: ```bash OPENYIDA_E2E=1 \ OPENYIDA_E2E_CONNECTOR=1 \ OPENYIDA_E2E_CORP_ID='<target-corp-id>' \ OPENYIDA_E2E_CONNECTOR_ECHO_URL='https://<team-controlled-host>/<stable-echo-path>' \ OPENYIDA_E2E_CONNECTOR_FIXTURE_MARKER='<expected-response-marker>' \ OPENYIDA_E2E_CONNECTOR_FIXTURE_OWNER='<expected-owner-header-value>' \ node scripts/e2e-real/connector/runner.js ``` The runner rejects public generic echo services such as httpbin and example.com. Before its first remote write it selects and verifies the explicit organization profile, prints a redacted resource plan, and persists synchronized registry/manifest evidence plus the SHA-256 of the preserved operations fixture. The controlled fixture must return exact JSON fields `content.runId`, `content.fixtureMarker`, and `content.authorization === "Basic ***"`, plus the exact `x-openyida-fixture-owner` response header. Substring matches, malformed JSON, and wrong fields fail closed. Each remote create is persisted as `attempted` before execution and becomes `completed` only after exact readback; an exception is recorded as `outcome_unknown` with a non-owned residual candidate and is never retried. The runner deletes only its temporary local copy and reports remote connector/account cleanup as blocked because the CLI has no proven delete API. If organization or fixture ownership cannot be proven, it returns `PLATFORM_PROBE_REQUIRED` with zero remote writes. The opt-in `node scripts/e2e-real/connector/action-update-runner.js` regression uses the owner-confirmed login-free `www.aliwork.com` fixture and a single owned NONE-auth connector containing a target action plus one preservation sentinel. Enable it with `OPENYIDA_E2E=1 OPENYIDA_E2E_CONNECTOR_ACTION_UPDATE=1`. It verifies isolated `currentPage`, `pageSize`, `userLanguage`, `searchFieldJson`, and dynamic `_stamp` edits, restores each field and the final baseline, and persists only response structure, data count, and SHA-256. It never stores response row values or auth/profile/corp identifiers, never retries unknown writes, and intentionally leaves the owned connector as a `cleanup_blocked` residual because no proven delete API exists. `openyida asset resolve --input manifest-draft.json --manifest asset-manifest.json --json` validates every image slot and writes a traceable manifest. Search assets only accept Unsplash/Pexels; draft results exit with code 2. Use `--offline` to block URL checks and uploads. #### Environment and Localization Environment selectors such as `--env intl`, `--intl`, `--overseas`, `--global`, and `--yidaapps` can be used on login-required commands to choose the target Yida environment for that run. The `intl` preset uses `https://www.yidaapps.com` as the built-in Global YiDA entrypoint (not the bare `https://yidaapps.com` domain) and DingTalk International OAuth at `https://login.dingtalk.io`; business API requests still use the authenticated environment `baseUrl`, so customer custom subdomains are supported. For overseas apps, pass `--locale en_US` or `--locale ja_JP` on creation commands, or set `OPENYIDA_CONTENT_LOCALE`. OpenYida writes YiDA resource names with `zh_CN`, `en_US`, and `ja_JP` values so Global YiDA does not fall back to Chinese-only metadata. The CLI package ships the core UI languages `zh` and `en` by default. Other CLI UI language packs are optional: keep or install files such as `ja.js` / `fr.js` in an external directory and point `OPENYIDA_LOCALE_DIR` to that directory, then set `OPENYIDA_LANG=ja`. If an optional language pack is unavailable, OpenYida falls back through `en -> zh`. #### Forms and Pages Form field definitions can include `alias` or `componentAlias` to populate Yida designer component aliases, stored as `pages[0].componentAlias.items`. Yida runtime resolves these aliases in page JS, so `this.$('phone')` can be used instead of `this.$('textField_xxx')`; OpenYida form rules, validations, and `openyida data ... --resolve-aliases` JSON inputs also accept aliases as field references. For server-side DingTalk OpenAPI calls, use `GET /v2.0/yida/forms/component/alias/{appType}/{formUuid}` to read the `{ fieldId, alias }` mapping, then translate aliases before sending form data/search JSON. That endpoint requires `systemToken`, `userId`, an access token, and the Yida form data read permission. Use `connector test --system-token-app <appType>` for a transient test or `integration create --connector-system-token-app <appType>` for a server-side automation; OpenYida resolves `systemToken` internally and never prints it or stores it in page source and Action defaults. `openyida publish` preserves existing custom page data sources by default. Before saving the new compiled JSX Schema, it reads the current page Schema and merges the Page-level `dataSource` with the built-in `urlParams` and `timestamp` sources, so manually configured data sources are not deleted during republish. #### Data, Permissions, and Sharing `openyida externalize-form` is useful when a form contains fields such as `AssociationFormField`, `EmployeeField`, or `DepartmentSelectField` that depend on internal organization permissions. It produces a report plus optional `--mirror-fields-output` JSON that can be used with `openyida create-form create` to build a separate public intake form while keeping the internal form and its association fields private. #### Workflow, Reports, and Integrations `openyida integration create` supports form events (`insert`, `update`, `delete`, `comment`) and approval events (`processFinish`, `activityTask`; aliases: `approval`, `approvalNode`). Approval events require `--approval-actions agree,disagree,terminated`; `activityTask` also requires `--approval-node-ids <nodeId,...>`. Passing `--process-code` selects a full graph replacement and now requires explicit `--replace`; it is not a safe update. `integration update` supports previewing and applying limited node patches to disabled automations with a trusted local baseline, including node names, descriptions and message titles/bodies. It checks the remote version, saves a backup and verifies the saved result. Without a trusted baseline or when the patch exceeds the supported fields, it returns `PLATFORM_PROBE_REQUIRED` without writing. See the [maintenance guide](yida-skills/skills/yida-integration/references/operations.md) for preview, fingerprint and publication examples. ### Connect a Local Agent Use an installed Qoder or Codex CLI on your computer to run tasks from the Yida web app. Local Agent supports macOS and Windows; the ordinary OpenYida CLI also supports Linux. Check your local environment, then follow the connection instructions in the Yida web app: ```bash openyida agent doctor --json ``` After connecting, the service runs in the background. Use `openyida agent status` to check its status, `openyida agent logs` to view logs, and `openyida agent disconnect` to disconnect. After restarting your computer, run `openyida agent run` to reconnect. ## Agent Skills The `yida-skills/` directory is the source skill library used by OpenYida during development and distributed with the npm package. | Path | Purpose | |------|---------| | `yida-skills/SKILL.md` | Entry point and skill index | | `yida-skills/skills/` | Self-contained sub-skills for app, form, process, page, data, and integration work | | `yida-skills/references/` | Shared Yida API, model API, and query-condition references | When OpenYida is used inside a supported AI coding environment, these skills help the agent choose the right command sequence and file conventions. For QwenWork, use the same user-level global skills layout as QoderWork: `~/.qwenworkcn/skills/yida-skills/`. Skip QwenWork setup when `~/.qwenworkcn` is not present. Qoder and Qoder IDE share the user-level `~/.qoder/skills/yida-skills/` directory. QoderWork remains a separate product and uses `~/.qoderwork/skills/yida-skills/`. For Codex, `npm install -g openyida` additionally creates a local plugin marketplace under `~/.openyida/codex-plugin` and enables `openyida@openyida` in `~/.codex/config.toml` when Codex is detected. This makes OpenYida show up in Codex's `@` plugin menu as **宜搭** after Codex reloads. ## Examples ### Business Systems: IPD and CRM Describe your requirements in one sentence; the agent can create a complete multi-form Yida application. ![IPD](https://img.alicdn.com/imgextra/i2/O1CN01YBEMa929J7sD9v8U1_!!6000000008046-2-tps-3840-3366.png) ![CRM](https://img.alicdn.com/imgextra/i3/O1CN01kn0Vcn1H5OkbQaizA_!!6000000000706-2-tps-3840-2168.png) ### Custom Pages and Utilities ![Salary Calculator](https://gw.alicdn.com/imgextra/i2/O1CN017TeJuE1reVH2Dj7b7_!!6000000005656-2-tps-5114-2468.png) ![Enterprise Collaboration](https://gw.alicdn.com/imgextra/i1/O1CN01EZtvfs1cxXV00UaXi_!!6000000003667-2-tps-5118-2470.png) ### Interactive Campaigns ![Lantern Riddle Game](https://img.alicdn.com/imgextra/i3/O1CN01dCoscP25jSAtAB9o3_!!6000000007562-2-tps-2144-1156.png) ## Common Prompts ```text Build a Yida application for [business scenario]. Generate an app from this requirements document. Create a [name] form page with these fields. Add a required [field type] field named [field name] to [form name]. Publish this custom page to the Yida app. Make this page publicly accessible. Export the application as a migration package. ``` ## OpenClaw Integration Use OpenYida through [yida-app](https://clawhub.ai/nicky1108/yida-app) in OpenClaw: ```bash npx clawhub@latest install nicky1108/yida-app ``` ## Development ```bash git clone https://github.com/openyida/openyida.git cd openyida nvm install nvm use npm ci --ignore-scripts npm run check:ci ``` Use the Node.js version in `.nvmrc` to match CI validation. If you do not use nvm, install that version directly. Useful checks: | Command | Purpose | |---------|---------| | `npm test` | Run Jest tests | | `npm run lint` | Run ESLint | | `npm run check:quick` | Run structure, manifest, syntax, and lint checks | | `npm run check:commands` | Validate router, command manifest, and README alignment | | `npm run docs:commands` | Regenerate the README command index from the manifest | | `npm run check:docs` | Verify generated README command docs are current | | `npm run check:syntax` | Validate JavaScript syntax | | `npm run check:structure` | Validate project structure | | `npm run check:package-size` | Validate npm package size and file-count budget | | `npm run check:package` | Validate npm package contents | When adding new CLI commands, register the route in `bin/yida.js`, add it to `lib/core/command-manifest.js`, regenerate the README command index with `npm run docs:commands`, and keep agent skills in `yida-skills/` aligned when the workflow changes. `npm run check:commands` fails if the router, manifest, or README drift apart. ## Security and Configuration - OAuth token sessions are cached locally and should never be hard-coded into source files. - Private deployment environments are managed through `lib/core/env-manager.js`. - Yida API requests should use the active environment base URL and Bearer token auth. - For multi-organization accounts, prefer explicit `--corp-id` values in non-interactive automation. ## Community Scan the QR code to join the OpenYida DingTalk user group for updates and support. ![Join OpenYida Community](https://img.alicdn.com/imgextra/i4/O1CN01RAlxmO1qF1cxRguyj_!!6000000005465-2-tps-350-356.png) ## Contributors Thanks to everyone who has contributed to OpenYida. items.description: Agentic Coding Rules, Templates etc...
items.readme_text: # Sam's Agentic Coding Rules, Templates and Examples - [Coding Agent Rules, Skills and Templates](#coding-agent-rules-skills-and-templates) - [Tips For Agentic Coding](#tips-for-agentic-coding) - [Recommended 3rd Party Plugins and Tools](#recommended-3rd-party-plugins-and-tools) - [Getting High Quality Outcomes \& Context Engineering](#getting-high-quality-outcomes--context-engineering) - [Subscription vs Consumption Based Providers](#subscription-vs-consumption-based-providers) - [Links](#links) - [License](#license) My Agent Skills, Agent Rules for Agentic Coding. ## Coding Agent Rules, Skills and Templates The repository is organised with tool-agnostic content at the root level: - [Agent Skills](./Skills/) - Composable skills that extend agent capabilities - [Custom Agents](./Claude/agents/) - Custom defined agents (use sparingly). - [Agent Rules](./Rules/) - Agent instruction files - [Rules/CLAUDE.md](./Rules/CLAUDE.md) is usually the most up to date and comprehensive - [Agent Commands](./Claude/commands/) - (Prompt templates) - [Claude Local Marketplace](./Claude/plugins/local-marketplace/) - My local marketplace (plugins) for Claude Code, including LSP definitions. Most skills and rules are reasonably portable between agentic coding tools. ![Setup -> Plan -> Act -> Review & Iterate Diagram](setup-plan-act-iterate.svg) --- ## Tips For Agentic Coding - Lean into [skills](https://github.com/sammcj/agentic-coding/tree/main/Skills), dynamical context acquisition is very powerful. - Read my [best practices and common pitfalls when writing and reviewing agent skills](https://smcleod.net/2026/07/writing-and-reviewing-agent-skills-common-pitfalls/). - If Claude gets stuck on a complex issue, get it to stop and perform a systematic debug of the issue using the systematic-debugging skill. - Setup your permissions (in settings.json) to pre-approve/deny/ask commands and file paths that Claude may want to use. - Always enable sandboxing for agent commands, ideally run your whole agent in a sandbox when it is practical to do so. - Encourage Claude to use sub-agents to parallelise work and keep context lean where it is safe to do so. - Using voice to text with a tool like [Handy](https://handy.computer/) to dictate work to Claude Code is incredibly useful, often with voice you capture intent that you'd otherwise edit out. - Create shell aliases for the various claude CLI commands you use, e.g. `alias cc='claude --continue`, `alias ccr='claude --resume` etc. - Add your context usage, and limits consumption to the statusline. - Only add rules (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md) for behaviour that is different from standard for the agent/model, keep them concise and review with an aim to reduce over time.Only enable the rules you actually want to use** - Don't waste time with low end models for planning or coding, the higher error rates, lower quality code and the rework they often incur does not pay off (at least with current generation models). ### Recommended 3rd Party Plugins and Tools - [cc-safety-net](https://ccsafetynet.com/) (hooks that try to catch some destructive commands). - [context-mode](https://github.com/mksglu/context-mode) which significantly reduces context usage. - [Graphify](https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify) can be useful for creating graphs of code and LLM wikis providing them with semantic search and context. Note: I do _not_ recommend using MCP tools like Github's where the agent is more than capable of using the gh cli or API directly, they tend to just waste tokens and bloat the context. --- ### Getting High Quality Outcomes & Context Engineering - Start with a plan - break down large or complex tasks into a checklist of items to complete, have the agent follow and mark off items has it completes them. - Relentlessly start fresh sessions, aim to keep the context under 200k - 300k max. - When you want to refresh the conversation ask the agent to document where it is up to and what's left to do (if you don't already have a dev plan with a checklist of tasks) and provide the document when starting a fresh session. - GIGO - Garbage In, Garbage Out. This aligns with the research that shows LLMs output correlates with the education level and quality of the input. - Make the system self-improving: If you spend a long time on a difficult problem with a coding agent and you finally crack it - get it to: 1. Summarise the fix 2. Why previous attempts did not work 3. What led them down the wrong paths initially 4. Suggest how to improve the agentic coding experience to prevent this in the future. - Understand that LLMs are stateless, this means that every time you send a message the entire context is sent back for re-processing. - Don't fall into the trap of thinking the solution is just around the corner when you've dug yourself into a hole troubleshooting, get the agent to document the problem, what it's tried to fix it so far and possible next things to try, then start a fresh session and provide the document. - Use checkpoints to roll back to previous points in the conversation or code changes when you've gone down the wrong path or want to explore a different approach. - Only use multimodal operations (images / screenshots as used by browser tools etc..) to a minimum - only when truly needed or where cost is not an issue as they use a lot of tokens. - Add files and directories you never want the agent to read to the agent's ignore file (e.g. `.clineignore` or claude.json's access rules). - Don't pipe data into LLMs and be wary of code with hardcoded data (XML, SVGs, i18n translations) inline. LLMs are designed to perform predictions (e.g. writing text / code and answering questions) effectively, they're not designed to parse large amounts of data at low cost - that's what software is for. --- ### Subscription vs Consumption Based Providers - A Claude Max 5 subscription will cost you $100 USD / month and get you over $1500+ equivalent worth of raw LLM API token usage, Max 20 gets you $2000-$5000~ worth. - Be wary of second tier subscription based AI coding tools, especially if they're built around an IDE like Cursor or Windsurf - they often provide you reduced versions of models with smaller context windows, artificially slowed response times and fallback to lower end models. Read the fine print especially if it seems too cheap to be true. - Some consumption based offerings like Github Copilot have very low rate limits if you use the service with anything other than their client. With Github Copilot's SDK you can use your entire months paid limits of Claude Sonnet access in just two days. --- ## Links - [Blog - smcleod.net](https://smcleod.net) - [GitHub - sammcj](https://github.com/sammcj) - [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code) - [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) - [Cline](https://cline.bot) ## License - This repository is licensed under the [Apache 2.0 License](./LICENSE).

items.name: MaxKB4j
items.description: MaxKB4j is an open-source LLMOps platform for LLM workflow applications and RAG developed based on the Java language. The project mainly draws on MaxKB, Dify and FastGPT, and combines the advantages of the two into one project. It is redesigned and developed using the high-performance, high-stability and secure reliable JAVA language.
items.readme_text:
🧠 MaxKB4j

Max Knowledge Brain for Java — an enterprise-grade AI brain for Java teams, with zero friction
An out-of-the-box, model-agnostic RAG + LLM workflow engine built on Java 21 + Spring Boot 3 (Virtual Threads)
Intelligent customer service · Enterprise knowledge bases · Data analysis · Research & education


[中文（简体）] | [English]

🚀 Quick Start · 🌐 Live Demo (demo / demo@123456) · 📄 Whitepaper · 🧪 Regression Report · 🗒️ Changelog · 💖 Support Us

--- ## Why Choose MaxKB4j? Enterprises face four common challenges when adopting LLM applications, and MaxKB4j answers each one: | Pain Point | MaxKB4j Answer | |:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | **Complex integration** — mainstream platforms rely on Python / TS ecosystems, making adoption costly for Java teams | **Pure Java native** — built on the Spring Boot 3 stack; existing Java engineers can extend it directly with zero cross-language cost | | **Serious hallucinations** — generic LLMs know nothing about internal enterprise data | **Production-grade RAG** — document parsing → chunking → vectorization → hybrid retrieval → Reranker re-ranking, with traceable answers | | **Concurrency bottlenecks** — traditional architectures cannot sustain high-concurrency Q&A | **Virtual Threads + reactive architecture** — thousands of concurrent requests per node with lower resource usage | | **Single-function Q&A** — no way to orchestrate complex business processes | **Visual workflow + Multi-Agent** — 30+ node types covering complex business scenarios | ## ✨ Key Capabilities | Capability | Description | |:-----------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | 🔍 Knowledge Base Q&A | Upload PDF / Word / TXT / Markdown files or crawl web pages; automatic chunking → vectorization → storage → RAG pipeline, significantly reducing hallucinations; in-document images are fused into vectors for image-text hybrid retrieval | | 🧠 Advanced RAG / AgenticRAG | Vector, full-text, and hybrid multi-route retrieval + Reranker re-ranking; agents dynamically decide retrieval paths with intent recognition and conditional branches, supporting multi-hop Q&A | | ⚙️ Visual Workflow | Low-code orchestration with 30+ node types: conditional branches, loops, variable aggregation, NL2SQL, forms, HTTP requests, MCP, etc.; multi-turn and long-term memory | | 🤝 Multi-Agent Collaboration | Multiple role-specific agents (data analyst, code reviewer, customer service agent…) work in parallel or sequence; tasks are decomposed, dispatched, and aggregated automatically via a shared memory bus | | ⏰ Triggers | Cron scheduled tasks + Webhook event callbacks for unattended automation (daily report generation, CRM-lead-triggered persona analysis, etc.) | | 🌐 Model-Agnostic | Private models via Ollama / Xorbits Inference / LocalAI; public models: Qwen, DeepSeek, Doubao, Hunyuan, GLM, Kimi, GPT, Claude, Gemini, and more | | 🧩 Seamless Integration | RESTful API, iframe / Web SDK embedding, OpenAI-compatible chat API, and stream_http MCP agent integration — connect within 5 minutes | | 🎙️ Multimodal | **Multimodal fusion embedding** — text and images in documents are fused into unified vectors, enabling text-to-image and image-to-text retrieval (Aliyun Bailian / Volcengine Ark vision embedding models); ASR speech recognition, TTS speech synthesis, OCR image recognition, Stable Diffusion image generation | | 🔒 Security & Permissions | Fine-grained permissions (application / knowledge base / tool / model) based on Sa-Token; audit logs; groovy-sandbox for safe script execution | | 🌱 Ecosystem Extensions | Dozens of pre-built agent templates (customer service assistant, data analyst, code mentor…); plugin marketplace: MySQL / PostgreSQL / MongoDB connectors, Feishu / DingTalk / WeCom integrations, web search tools | ## 📊 How MaxKB4j Compares | Capability | **MaxKB4j** | Dify | MaxKB | FastGPT | RAGFlow | |:-------------------------------------|:---------------------------:|:-----------:|:------:|:----------:|:-------:| | Backend stack | **Java 21 + Spring Boot 3** | Python + TS | Python | TypeScript | Python | | Zero language-switch for Java teams | ✅ Native | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | | Virtual-Thread high concurrency | ✅ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | | Visual workflow + Multi-Agent | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | | Triggers (Cron / Webhook) | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | | Multimodal (ASR / TTS / OCR) | ✅ | ⚠️ | ✅ | ⚠️ | ✅ | | Text + image fusion embedding | ✅ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | | MCP protocol / OpenAI-compatible API | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | > Note: this table is a capability-orientation comparison for selection reference. Evaluate with your own scenarios via > the live demo below. ## 🚀 Quick Start ### Requirements - Java 21+ - PostgreSQL 12+ (with pgvector extension enabled) - MongoDB 6.0+ (full-text search and file storage) ### Option 1: Docker Compose (recommended) ```bash docker-compose up -d ``` Then open `http://localhost:8080/admin/login` (default `admin` / `tarzan@123456`). The database is initialized automatically on first startup. ### Option 2: Docker single container ```bash docker run --name maxkb4j -d --restart always -p 8080:8080 \ -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/MaxKB4j \ -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=postgres \ -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=123456 \ -e SPRING_DATA_MONGODB_URI=mongodb://admin:123456@localhost:27017/MaxKB4j?authSource=admin \ registry.cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/tarzanx/maxkb4j ``` ### Option 3: One-click install script Interactive installers in `deploy/` handle environment checks, image pulling / building, and docker-compose orchestration (Linux / macOS / Windows): ```bash # Linux / macOS chmod +x deploy/install.sh ./deploy/install.sh # Windows deploy\install.bat ``` ### Option 4: Build from source ```bash mvn clean package -DskipTests java -jar maxkb4j-start/target/maxkb4j-start.jar ``` Profiles: `maxkb4j-start/src/main/resources/application-{dev,prod,test}.yml`, switch with `--spring.profiles.active=dev`. ### Deploy to cloud platforms Supports one-click deployment to [Sealos](https://blog.csdn.net/weixin_40986713/article/details/156026021) (overseas servers, no proxy needed, auto-scaling). > 🎉 **Deployed successfully?** > If MaxKB4j saved your team development time, consider [buying the author a coffee ☕](#support--sponsorship) — a coffee > unlocks the author's direct WeChat line and the core community group, where deployment questions get answered fast. ## 🌐 Live Demo - Live demo: http://43.143.235.194:8080/ (account `demo` / password `demo@123456`, normal-user permissions) - Local default admin: `admin` / `tarzan@123456` ## 🛠 Tech Stack & Project Structure | Category | Tech | |:---------------|:--------------------------------------------------------| | Backend | Java 21, Spring Boot 3, Virtual Threads, Sa-Token | | AI framework | LangChain4j 1.x, Docling document parsing, Volcengine Ark SDK | | Storage | PostgreSQL 15 + pgvector, MongoDB 6.0+, Caffeine cache | | Frontend | Element Plus,Vue 3, Node.js v20.16.0 | | Script sandbox | groovy-sandbox | ``` MaxKB4j/ ├── maxkb4j-common / maxkb4j-core # Utilities, core abstractions, domain models ├── maxkb4j-service/ # Business implementation: application / chat / knowledge / model / oss / system / tool / trigger / workflow ├── maxkb4j-service-api/ # Public contracts: -api modules (DTOs / VOs) ├── maxkb4j-start/ # Spring Boot entry point, config, packaging └── deploy/ # One-click install scripts (install.sh / install.bat) ``` > Dependency direction: `start` → `service` → `service-api` → `core` → `common`. Public contracts live in `-api` > modules; implementations live in `service`. ## 📄 Documentation & Resources - 📄 [Business Value Whitepaper](docs/MaxKB4j-商业价值白皮书.md) — value and selection analysis for enterprise decision makers - 🧪 [Regression Test Report](docs/MaxKB4j-回归测试报告.md) — regression verification results of core features - 📐 [Coding Conventions](docs/编码约定.md) - 🗒️ [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md) — latest release: v2.9.0 (2026-06-17) ## 🤝 Contributing | Item | Details | |:--------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | Feedback & requests | Report bugs, suggestions, or feature requests via [Gitee Issues](https://gitee.com/taisan/MaxKB4j/issues) | | Contribution flow | Fork → create a branch → push to the DEV branch → open a Pull Request | | Coding standards | Follow Alibaba Java coding conventions; include unit tests and update docs | ## 💖 Support & Sponsorship > **MaxKB4j has no commercial backing and no funding** — it is built line by line by an independent developer in his > spare time. > Every contribution goes directly to real costs: > > - 🖥 **Cloud servers for the live demo** — running 24/7, free for everyone to try > - 🤖 **Model token consumption** — every regression test costs real money > - 🧪 **Bug fixes & new feature development** — caffeine for late-night coding > > Usage is reported regularly in the community group, fully transparent. > > ⚠️ The author's time is limited: **direct WeChat access and the core community group are reserved for sponsors** (from > ¥10) — this protects both the author's focus and the signal quality of the group. ### Sponsorship Tiers | Tier | Amount | Benefits | Best for | |:---------------------:|:------:|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------| | ☕ Coffee | ¥10 | Direct WeChat line to the author + core community group + AI Agent starter course | Anyone who appreciates the project | | 📚 Learning Member | ¥99 | All Coffee benefits + free access to the [Knowledge Planet](https://wx.zsxq.com/group/28882525858841) + priority answers inside the planet | Developers who want to master RAG / workflow in practice | | 🏢 Enterprise Partner | ¥798 | All Learning Member benefits + frontend source code (one-time) + deployment / post-sales support | Teams going to production | | 👑 Strategic Partner | ¥1398 | All Enterprise Partner benefits + 6-month frontend source upgrades + your logo on the sponsor wall | Long-term partners growing together | > 💡 **Every tier includes the author's direct WeChat line + the core community group** — unlocked from the ¥10 Coffee > tier. ### How to Sponsor (3 steps)

items.readme_text:
Zhin.js

Write a chat bot once in TypeScript. Run it on 20+ platforms.
QQ · WeChat · WeCom · DingTalk · Lark · Discord · Telegram · Slack · KOOK · LINE · …

English · 简体中文

Documentation · Live Demo · Remote Console · Wiki · Contributing

--- ## What is Zhin.js? Zhin.js is a framework for building **bots that live in chat apps** — community bots, personal assistants, notification and support bots, AI chat assistants. - **One codebase, many platforms.** Adapters translate each platform into one unified message, so your commands and replies work everywhere. One bot can run many accounts on many platforms at once. - **A feature is a file.** `commands/hello/index.ts` *is* the `/hello` command. Middleware, message cards, scheduled jobs and AI tools work the same way — no registration boilerplate. - **Small by default, AI when you want it.** The IM core is under 10MB and needs no model key. Add LLMs, tools, memory and MCP with one command. - **Hot reload that can't take you down.** Save a file and the bot reloads. If the new code fails, the previous version keeps serving. - **Managed from the browser.** [console.zhin.dev](https://console.zhin.dev) lets you send test messages, read logs, edit config and manage plugins — nothing to deploy. > Zhin is **not** an in-editor coding agent (like Cursor or Claude Code). Its AI features exist to power bots on chat platforms. ## Quick start No platform account and no model key required. ```bash npm create zhin-app my-bot -y cd my-bot pnpm dev ``` 1. Open [console.zhin.dev](https://console.zhin.dev). 2. Enter the API address printed in the terminal (new projects use `http://127.0.0.1:8068`) and the `HTTP_TOKEN` from `.env`. 3. Open the **Sandbox** chat and send `/hello`. You should get a reply. `-y` accepts every default: a browser **Sandbox** (simulated chat) instead of a real platform, and no AI. Requirements: Node.js **≥22.19.0** and pnpm 9+. Something wrong? Run `npx zhin doctor`. Full walkthrough: [Quick start](./docs/en/getting-started/index.md) · Prefer not to install yet? Try the [live demo](https://demo.zhin.dev). > [!IMPORTANT] > **Upgrading an existing bot from 1.1.13 or earlier?** The Runtime now only accepts `configVersion: 2`. Stop the Bot first, upgrade `zhin.js` / `@zhin.js/cli` to the latest, then run `zhin migrate instances` (preview) and `zhin migrate instances --apply` (backs up first). Full steps and restore: [Upgrading to configVersion 2](./docs/en/operations/upgrades.md#configversion-2). ## How a bot is put together ```text chat platform your project (a plugin) chat platform QQ / Discord … ──▶ Adapter ──▶ Middleware ──▶ Command ──────────────▶ Adapter ──▶ reply │ no command matched └──▶ AI Agent (optional) ──▶ Tools ``` | Part | What it is | Where it lives | |------|------------|----------------| | **Plugin** | Your project *is* a plugin; split it into child plugins as it grows | `plugin.ts` + the `zhin` field in `package.json` | | **Command** | Runs when a user sends `/hello` | `commands/hello/index.ts` | | **Middleware** | Sees every message — keyword replies, filters | `middlewares//index.ts` | | **Adapter** | An npm package connecting one platform; one adapter can host many accounts | `@zhin.js/adapter-*`, configured in `zhin.config.yml` | | **AI Agent** *(optional)* | Answers messages no command matched, and can call your tools | `tools//index.ts`, `ai:` in `zhin.config.yml` | | **Console** | Browser admin UI for logs, config and test messages | [console.zhin.dev](https://console.zhin.dev) | New to these terms? Read [Core concepts at a glance](./docs/en/getting-started/concepts.md) — it explains every word the docs use, in plain language. ## Writing features A whole bot can be one file: ```ts // bot.ts import { definePlugin } from 'zhin.js' import { defineCommand } from 'zhin.js/command' export default definePlugin({ name: 'my-bot', setup({ addCommand }) { addCommand('hello', defineCommand({ description: 'Say hello', execute: () => 'Hello from Zhin!', })) }, }) ``` As it grows, move each capability into its own file. The folder path is the name, and the file registers itself: ```ts // commands/remind/index.ts → /remind 10 stretch import { defineCommand } from 'zhin.js/command' export default defineCommand({ description: 'Create a reminder', params: { minutes: { type: 'integer', min: 1, max: 1440 }, note: { type: 'text', default: 'Take a break' }, }, options: { quiet: { type: 'boolean', default: false } }, // --quiet execute: ({ params, options }) => options.quiet ? 'OK' : `OK, I'll remind you in ${params.minutes} min: ${params.note}`, }) ``` ```text my-bot/ ├── package.json # "zhin" field: entry and child plugins (what is installed) ├── zhin.config.yml # port, platform credentials, models (how it is configured) ├── .env # secrets: HTTP_TOKEN, API keys ├── plugin.ts # entry: definePlugin() ├── commands/ # /commands — folder path = command name ├── middlewares/ # runs on every message ├── components/ # reusable JSX message cards ├── schedules/ # scheduled jobs ├── tools/ # functions the AI may call (optional) └── pages/ # custom Console pages ``` Next: [Write your first plugin](./docs/en/getting-started/first-plugin.md) · [All convention folders](./docs/en/authoring/conventions.md) · [Commands in depth](./docs/en/authoring/commands.md) ## Connect a real platform ```bash npx zhin setup --adapters # pick platforms, enter credentials pnpm install && pnpm dev ``` | Platform | Package | Platform | Package | |----------|---------|----------|---------| | Sandbox (local testing) | `@zhin.js/adapter-sandbox` | QQ (ICQQ) | `@zhin.js/adapter-icqq` | | QQ official bot | `@zhin.js/adapter-qq` | OneBot v11 / v12 | `@zhin.js/adapter-onebot11` / `onebot12` | | Discord | `@zhin.js/adapter-discord` | Telegram | `@zhin.js/adapter-telegram` | | Slack | `@zhin.js/adapter-slack` | KOOK | `@zhin.js/adapter-kook` | | DingTalk | `@zhin.js/adapter-dingtalk` | Lark / Feishu | `@zhin.js/adapter-lark` | | WeCom | `@zhin.js/adapter-wecom` | WeChat MP | `@zhin.js/adapter-wechat-mp` | | LINE | `@zhin.js/adapter-line` | NapCat / Milky / Satori | `napcat` / `milky` / `satori` | | Email | `@zhin.js/adapter-email` | GitHub | `@zhin.js/adapter-github` | Each adapter has a maturity tier (Stable / Advanced / Experimental) and its own setup guide: [Adapters overview](./docs/en/adapters/index.md). ## Add AI (optional) ```bash npx zhin setup --ai # choose a provider (OpenAI, Ollama, …) and write the config pnpm install && pnpm dev ``` The wizard installs the Agent runtime and the tool / prompt features, and writes something like this to `zhin.config.yml` (keys go to `.env`): ```yaml ai: enabled: true providers: openai-main: sdk: openai apiKey: ${AI_API_KEY} agents: zhin: provider: openai-main model: gpt-4o-mini ``` Messages that match no command now go to the model — in DMs by default, in groups with an `ai:` prefix or a mention. Give it abilities by adding files to `tools/`; permissions, approvals and file/network access are enforced by framework policy, not by the prompt. Next: [AI overview](./docs/en/ai/index.md) · [Agent tools, Skills and Prompt Sections](./docs/en/authoring/agent-tools.md) · [AI Agent learning path](./docs/en/paths/ai-agent.md) ## Install only what you need | Tier | Install | Adds | |------|---------|------| | **IM** (default) | `zhin.js` + an adapter; `@zhin.js/cli` for dev | Plugins, commands, middleware, components, adapters, hot reload — **<10MB** | | **AI** | `npx zhin setup --ai` (installs `@zhin.js/agent` and features) | Agent, sessions, memory, tools, compaction | | **Provider** | `@ai-sdk/openai` etc. | Calls to a specific LLM vendor | | **MCP** | `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` | Use tools from external MCP servers | | **Rich media** | `@zhin.js/html-renderer` | Render HTML / Markdown replies to images (falls back to text) | | **Speech** | `@zhin.js/speech` | Speech-to-text in, text-to-speech out | Detailed table and sizes: [Install tiers](./docs/en/getting-started/index.md#install-tiers). Since 1.1, `ZhinAgent` / `AIService` are imported from `zhin.js/agent` / `zhin.js/ai`, not from `zhin.js`. ## Documentation | I want to… | Start here | |------------|------------| | Understand what Zhin is | [What is Zhin.js](./docs/en/getting-started/introduction.md) · [Core concepts](./docs/en/getting-started/concepts.md) | | Run a bot for the first time | [Quick start](./docs/en/getting-started/index.md) · [Examples](./docs/en/examples/index.md) | | Write plugins | [First plugin](./docs/en/getting-started/first-plugin.md) · [definePlugin](./docs/en/authoring/define-plugin.md) · [Plugin delivery (test & publish)](./docs/en/authoring/plugin-delivery.md) | | Connect platforms | [Adapters](./docs/en/adapters/index.md) · [Configuration](./docs/en/configuration/index.md) | | Add AI | [AI overview](./docs/en/ai/index.md) · [Agent deep dive](./docs/en/ai/agent.md) | | Deploy and operate | [Production](./docs/en/operations/production.md) · [Console](./docs/en/console/index.md) · [Troubleshooting](./docs/en/troubleshooting/index.md) | | Understand the internals | [Architecture](./docs/en/concepts/architecture.md) · [Plugin model](./docs/en/concepts/plugin-model.md) · [Message flow](./docs/en/concepts/message-flow.md) · [Hot reload (Generations)](./docs/en/concepts/generation-lifecycle.md) | Full site: [zhin.js.org](https://zhin.js.org) (Chinese by default; switch language in the nav). ## CLI cheat sheet ```bash npx zhin setup # add platforms, AI, database to an existing project npx zhin doctor # diagnose Node, ports, tokens, manifest npx @zhin.js/cli new my-plugin --standalone # scaffold a publishable plugin package npx zhin search # find community plugins npx zhin install # install and mount a plugin ``` All commands: [CLI reference](./docs/en/cli/index.md). ## Packages | Package | What it is | |---------|------------| | [`zhin.js`](./packages/im/zhin) | The package you install — re-exports everything plugin authors need | | [`create-zhin-app`](./packages/toolkit/create-zhin) | Project scaffolder (`npm create zhin-app`) | | [`@zhin.js/cli`](./basic/cli) | The `zhin` command: run, set up, diagnose, publish | | [`@zhin.js/agent`](./packages/im/agent) | Optional AI Agent runtime with security policies | | [`@zhin.js/adapter-*`](./plugins/adapters) | Platform adapters | | [`plugins/`](./plugins) | Official plugins: games, reminders, RSS, calendar, moderation… | How the layers fit together: [architecture](./docs/en/concepts/architecture.md) · [repo structure](./docs/contributing/repo-structure.md). ## Contributing ```bash git clone https://github.com/zhinjs/zhin.git cd zhin pnpm install && pnpm build pnpm dev # runs examples/minimal-bot ``` Other entry points: `pnpm --filter single-file-bot dev` (one-file bot) and `pnpm dev:test` (maintainers' kitchen-sink `test-bot`, not a template). See the [contributing guide](./docs/contributing/development.md) for checks, conventions and the release flow.

items.name: berth
items.description: Decides who gets your GPU. Chat, image and voice engines lease the card in turn instead of grabbing it, so two of them never load at once and crash each other. One Go binary, nothing else to install.
items.readme_text:
Quick start · How it works · Install · Gateway · Harbor · Roadmap

# Berth Berth makes the programs on your PC take turns with the GPU's memory, so they stop crashing each other, and tells you who is holding it. Berth decides who gets your GPU. Chat models, image pipelines, voice engines, games and GPU apps lease the card instead of grabbing it, so two of them never load at once and crash each other with an out-of-memory error. One Go binary, no cloud account, nothing else to install. ```sh berth daemon & # one broker per card berth run --as llama -- llama-server -m model.gguf # this engine now takes turns berth status # who holds the card, who waits, and why ``` ## How it works

Every engine asks berthd for the card: through `berth run`, the gateway, ComfyUI's API or a game claim. When another engine holds it, Berth: 1. queues the request by priority: `hold`, `foreground`, `interactive`, `batch`; 2. lets the holder finish its reply or image job, then unloads it; 3. waits until the driver shows the memory free; 4. grants the lease and starts the next engine, and the request that waited streams. The numbered markers on the timeline are those four steps. A process that holds VRAM without a lease shows up as a stowaway: Berth reports its PID and memory and leaves it running. > **Status: alpha, v0.3.1.** Runs daily on an RTX 4090 workstation beside llama-swap, NInfer, > Strata, ComfyUI and games, and testers run it on Windows. [Capabilities](#capabilities) lists what works and has tests; the > [Roadmap](#roadmap) lists the phases and what is still missing. ### Berth and llama-swap Use both. llama-swap swaps the models in its own config, and does it well. Berth governs the whole card: llama-swap's models, ComfyUI, Ollama, vLLM, games, and any process that holds VRAM, including the ones neither tool started. With Berth beside it, llama-swap's next model waits for ComfyUI or the engine before it to give the memory back, and when a crashed process still holds part of the card, Berth names its PID and how much it holds, so you aren't hunting through `nvidia-smi` while a load fails. `berth wire llama-swap` adds the lease to every model in your config in one pass. An upstream integration with llama-swap is planned, so the wrapper line goes away. ## What Berth does **Shares one card between everything** - **Engines take turns.** You start each one through `berth run`. When another needs the card, Berth waits for the holder's current reply to end, unloads it (its own unload, then SIGTERM, then SIGKILL) and lets the next one in only after the driver shows the memory free. - **Priorities.** `foreground`, `interactive`, `batch`, and `hold` above them all. A lower request waits and gets a reason naming the holder, never an OOM crash. - **No ping-pong.** When two clients ask for different engines at once, a ranking picks one and the other waits, so the card stays put. - **ComfyUI at a job boundary.** Berth waits for the running image job to finish before the handoff. - **A minimum turn.** `min_turn = "5m"` keeps an engine on the card for five minutes after it gets it, whatever asks next; only a hold takes it out sooner. - **Engines in containers.** `berth run --container NAME -- docker run ...` puts a Docker or Podman engine under its lease, and the drain stops it through `docker stop`. - **Survives restarts.** Upgrade or restart the daemon and your running engines stay up and re-attach. The gateway's engines survive it too: it starts each one as its own `berth run` process (in its own systemd scope on Linux) and adopts them again on its next start. **Faster switches, and a way out** *(v0.3)* - **Park in RAM.** An engine that can offload itself (ComfyUI, vLLM, SGLang, or any engine that serves the [park protocol](contrib/PARK-PROTOCOL.md)) moves its weights to system memory on a drain and resumes from there instead of reloading from disk. Berth parks only when the RAM it measures covers the engine plus a floor, and stops parked engines first when memory runs short. - **A way out of every lease state.** `berth stop ENGINE` drains an engine on purpose, `berth resume ENGINE` puts a parked one back, and `berth reclaim` stops what a stuck release left behind, once you confirm. - **A place in the queue.** Every wait reason starts with the waiter's place ("2nd in line (behind interactive comfyui)"), and `berth status` adds a start estimate from measured switches. **Games and other apps** - **Games take the card while you play.** Launch a Steam, Lutris or gamescope game on Linux, or a Steam, Epic, GOG, EA, Ubisoft, Xbox or Battle.net game on Windows, and Berth drains your AI engines until you quit. - **Creative apps keep their memory.** Berth names what Blender, DaVinci Resolve, OBS, Kdenlive, Premiere and After Effects hold and counts it against the card, without a stowaway report. - **Your own rules.** `[[claim]]` in `berth.toml` covers anything else: a training run, a render farm job, a cracking session, by name, command line or launcher. - **`berth hold`** frees the card for a call or a game you start yourself. Ctrl-C gives it back. - **`berth run --pinned`** for an app that must never be stopped mid-work. **One API for your engines** *(preview)* - **`berth gateway`**: one OpenAI-compatible port. Name a model and Berth starts its engine, unloads whatever holds the card, waits for the load and streams the answer. - It proxies ComfyUI's workflow API too, so an image request queues behind the same lease. - **Wake pages** (`--gui-listen`): a bookmark to a stopped engine's web UI shows who holds the card and a Start button, says what the start waits for, and opens the UI once it answers. - Bearer key on every API route, loopback only, browser origins refused. **Models** - **`berth pull hf:org/repo:Q4_K_M`** downloads from Hugging Face, resumes where it stopped, and checks every file against the size and sha256 the Hub publishes before using it. - **`berth pull civitai:VERSION_ID`** does the same from CivitAI, with the hash the site publishes, and **`berth models`** shelves what it finds as chat, image or audio so a machine reading a shared root knows what a folder is. - **`berth storage`** shows each model root's filesystem, free space against its floor, and the other operating systems it is shared with. - **`berth verify`** re-checks pulled models offline and names any file that changed. - **`berth models`** lists every model on the machine (GGUF, safetensors, the Hugging Face cache, LM Studio and Ollama's stores) with quant, size, parameters, context and when each was last used, so you can see what earns its disk space. - **`berth models export ollama`** turns a GGUF you already have into an Ollama model. **Keeps itself current** - **`berth update`** asks the release page whether a newer berth exists and, when one does, downloads this machine's binary and the release's SHA256SUMS, checks the hash, and replaces the running binary in place after you confirm. It then names what to restart; it never restarts anything itself. - **Update check.** The harbor asks GitHub at most once every 24 h, one GET to the API's releases/latest, cached in the state directory, and shows "Update available" in its header when the answer is a newer release. `[update] check = false` in `berth.toml` turns the check off, and with it off Berth never contacts GitHub on its own. `berth update` and `berth update --check` ask GitHub every time you type them and never read the harbor's cached answer. **Sees everything on the card** - **Finds your engines.** Berth reads llama.cpp, llama-swap, Ollama, vLLM, SGLang, ComfyUI, Kokoro, LM Studio, KoboldCpp, TabbyAPI, LocalAI and more on their default ports, plus any OpenAI-compatible or custom server you name. - **Stowaways.** Berth reports any process holding VRAM without a lease, with its PID, name and memory, and leaves it running. - **Built-in telemetry.** Per-card memory, load, temperature, power and clocks; tokens per second, queue, latency percentiles, KV cache use, a token ledger and a per-model leaderboard; 30 days of history on disk. - **The harbor web UI** (`berth harbor`): a departures board of leases, a collisions-avoided counter, charts and the event log. Read-only, loopback by default. - **Alerts** to the desktop or a webhook, `/metrics` for Prometheus, and `berth export` for CSV or JSON. **Built for agents and scripts** - **`berth skill install`** teaches Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and other agents to ask Berth for the card instead of killing GPU processes. - Every reporting command takes `--format json|yaml`. All of them keep results on stdout and diagnostics on stderr, and exit 0, 1 or 2 by one rule. **Runs on** Linux with an NVIDIA GPU (supported) and Windows 10/11 with an NVIDIA GPU (experimental). Apache-2.0. ## Quick start ```sh go install github.com/T-Crypt/berth/cmd/berth@latest # or a release binary, see Install berth service install --harbor # berthd and the harbor, as user services berth status # the card, leases, the engines and their estimated VRAM berth run --as llama --priority foreground -- llama-server -m model.gguf --port 8080 ``` On Linux the services are systemd user units; on Windows they are Task Scheduler logon tasks that need no admin and run in your session, where your GPU apps are. The harbor answers on http://127.0.0.1:9798/. `berth service status` shows them and `berth service uninstall` removes them; the manual steps in Install do the same by hand. The harbor and gateway take their addresses from berth.toml when their `--listen` flags are not given: `[harbor] listen` and `[gateway] listen`, so a port change is a config edit and a restart of the service, not a reinstall. On Windows, installing also starts the tasks it creates, and each task appends its output to a log file under the state directory, which `berth service status` prints. ## Preview The harbor UI (basic mode, served from the built-in demo fixture - every number on the screen comes from `demo.json`). The tide shows the card's memory by holder over six hours; the hatched stretch is a stowaway the fixture replays: a model that ran without a lease after a daemon restart, reported and left alone.

The Engines tab (advanced mode): the engine cards with their learned footprints as EST. VRAM, the library (shelf, quant, size, the cached tier, the serving engine), decode throughput, the token ledger, the per-model leaderboard, storage and residency.

On a phone, the harbor fits the screen: the tabs move to a bar at the bottom and the panels stack. This is the CARD tab on an iPhone, read from a live node on the reference workstation.

### The harbor on your iPhone's Home Screen The harbor listens on loopback, so first give your phone a way to reach it. On a tailnet, publish it from the Berth machine and pass the name it serves under to the harbor: ```sh tailscale serve --bg --https=443 http://127.0.0.1:9798 berth harbor --allow-host ..ts.net ``` Then, on the iPhone: 1. Open `https://..ts.net/` in Safari. 2. Tap Share, then **Add to Home Screen**. 3. Name it (`berth` works) and tap **Add**. The Home Screen icon is Pilot, the harbor master llama, and the name under it is `berth`. The page stays read-only. The harbor has no login, so publish it only on a tailnet or a home network you trust. ## Install Two ways: hand it to your coding agent, or do it yourself. Both end in the same place: the daemon running as a user service, your engines wrapped in `berth run`, and the harbor UI on . ### Option 1: have your agent install it Paste this into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode or any coding agent that can run shell commands on the machine with the GPU: ```text Install Berth (https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth), a VRAM lease broker for NVIDIA GPUs, on this Linux machine, following its README and contrib/INTEGRATION.md. Steps: 1. Check prerequisites: Linux, an NVIDIA driver with `nvidia-smi` working, systemd user services. Stop and tell me if any is missing. 2. Download the latest release binary for this CPU (berth-linux-amd64 or berth-linux-arm64) and its SHA256SUMS from https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth/releases/latest, verify the checksum, and install it as ~/.local/bin/berth. (If Go 1.27+ is installed you may instead run: go install github.com/T-Crypt/berth/cmd/berth@latest.) Run `berth version`. 3. Run `berth service install --harbor`. It writes the systemd user units (the files in contrib/) with your binary's path in place of the one they name, and starts them; a unit file that already differs is kept as .bak (on Windows: a task whose XML differs). Confirm with `berth status`. 4. Find the inference engines on this machine (llama.cpp, llama-swap, Ollama, vLLM, SGLang, ComfyUI, LM Studio, KoboldCpp, TabbyAPI, LocalAI and so on): what runs them (systemd unit, llama-swap config, script) and on which port. Show me the list before changing anything. 5. For each engine I approve, wrap its start command in `berth run` as contrib/INTEGRATION.md shows (ComfyUI: contrib/comfyui.service with --drain-comfyui; Ollama: a systemd override of `ollama serve`). For llama-swap, wire the whole roster in one pass instead of one model at a time: `berth wire llama-swap --config --write` keeps a backup beside the file, keeps each model's original command, and `--check` exits 1 when a model is unwired. Ask me which engine wins the card (--priority foreground) and which waits (interactive or batch). Back up every file before you edit it and tell me how to undo each change. 6. Engines on non-default ports or other machines: add [[engine]] entries or [engines] discover_ports / discover_hosts to ~/.config/berth/berth.toml, then run `berth config check` and `berth engine check`. 7. Restart what you changed, then show me `berth status` with each engine leased and read, and the harbor at http://127.0.0.1:9798/. Do not expose the harbor beyond loopback unless I ask; it has no authentication. ``` The agent asks before it wraps anything, and every change it makes has an undo. ### Option 2: manual **1. The binary.** Download `berth-linux-amd64` (or `-arm64`) and `SHA256SUMS` from the [latest release](https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth/releases/latest): ```sh cd /tmp curl -fLO https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth/releases/latest/download/berth-linux-amd64 curl -fLO https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth/releases/latest/download/SHA256SUMS sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS install -Dm755 berth-linux-amd64 ~/.local/bin/berth berth version ``` Or build it: `go install github.com/T-Crypt/berth/cmd/berth@latest` (Go 1.27+, no C toolchain). **2. The daemon and the UI** (one per machine). `berth service install --harbor` does this on both platforms; by hand, on Linux, they are systemd user units from `contrib/`: ```sh mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user cp contrib/berthd.service contrib/berth-harbor.service ~/.config/systemd/user/ systemctl --user daemon-reload systemctl --user enable --now berthd berth-harbor berth status # the card, leases, stowaways, the engines and their estimated VRAM ``` Open . Engines on their default ports appear on their own. **3. Wrap your engines** so they lease the card instead of grabbing it. The pattern: ```sh berth run --as --priority -- ``` Per-engine recipes (llama-swap, llama.cpp, Ollama, ComfyUI, vLLM, SGLang, custom) are in [contrib/INTEGRATION.md](contrib/INTEGRATION.md). **4. Optional configuration** in `~/.config/berth/berth.toml`; validate with `berth config check`: ```toml [metrics] listen = "127.0.0.1:9797" # Prometheus text, loopback only [harbor] # listen = "127.0.0.1:9798" # where `berth harbor` listens; a LAN address exposes the web UI (no auth) [engines] # discover = true # default: probe the well-known engine ports every minute # discover_ports = [9123] # extra ports to probe # discover_hosts = ["192.168.1.40"] [[engine]] # anything discovery does not find, on any port name = "llama-swap" type = "llama-swap" url = "http://127.0.0.1:9090" [alerts] [alerts.queue] warn = 4 crit = 10 [models] # dirs = ["/mnt/d/models"] # the roots berth models scans and pull writes into [library] # free_floor = 0.10 # keep this fraction of every root free; 0 turns it off [[library.root]] # what a root holds and shares path = "/mnt/d/models" shelf = "image" # chat | image | audio; beats what the files say shared = "windows" # the other side of a shared root, shown by berth storage ``` **Uninstall:** `systemctl --user disable --now berthd berth-harbor`, remove the two unit files and `~/.local/bin/berth`, and take `berth run ... --` off any engine command you wrapped. History lives in `~/.local/state/berth/`. --- ## Engines | Engine | Reader (`type`) | Found on its own | What Berth reads | |---|---|---|---| | llama.cpp `llama-server` | `llamacpp` | :8080 | tokens, rates, queue, context window, KV slots | | llama-swap | `llama-swap` | :8080 | every running model's upstream, request log, per-model window | | Ollama | `ollama` | :11434 | loaded models and their VRAM | | vLLM | `vllm` | :8000 | models, window; tokens and queue from `/metrics` | | SGLang | `sglang` | :30000 | models, window; tokens and queue with `--enable-metrics` | | ComfyUI | `comfyui` | :8188 | jobs running and queued, version; job-boundary handoff | | Kokoro-FastAPI (text to speech) | `kokoro` | :8880 | health, models, voice count, default voice | | LM Studio | `lmstudio` | :1234 | loaded models, context length | | KoboldCpp | `koboldcpp` | :5001 | model, context length | | TabbyAPI (ExLlamaV3) | `tabbyapi` | :5000 | models, context length | | LocalAI | `localai` | :8080 | models, tokens | | Unsloth Studio | `unsloth` | :8888 | health; models with an API key | | FreeToken | `freetoken` | :1919 | tokens, queue | | [NInfer](https://github.com/T-Crypt/ninfer-4090) | `ninfer` | as llama.cpp | as llama.cpp, plus draft acceptance | | [Strata](https://github.com/T-Crypt/strata) | `strata` | :8080 | model, window, tokens, queue | | Any OpenAI-compatible server | `openai` | :8080, :8000 | models | | Anything else | `custom` | never | your health, models, metrics and slots paths; `kind = "tts"`, `"stt"`, `"image"` or `"other"` tracks a voice or image server as one | Every reader takes any URL, so any port and any host works. Engines that need a key name the environment variable that holds it (`api_key_env`); the key never goes in the config. On Unix, `api_key_file` instead names an absolute, owner-private regular file containing one token. Symlinks and files accessible to other users are rejected. The two sources are mutually exclusive. `berth run --api-key-file` uses the same source for drain requests; detached gateway launches pass the source reference, never its contents. Other platforms use `api_key_env` and explicitly reject file credentials. An engine's figures are its own claims and are shown apart from what the driver measures. ### ComfyUI as a suite `berth engine install|show|update|rollback|remove` manages ComfyUI as a suite: the core, ComfyUI-Manager and every git-based node pack are separate components, each pinned to a git commit with one previous commit kept as the rollback snapshot. Several installs run side by side on separate ports; each install's derived engine appears in `berth engine check`, `berth status` and the gateway's wake page, and its start line is the exact `berth run` shape an operator's unit already uses (the only alignment needed is `--as `). - `install NAME --adopt PATH` records an existing checkout in place; `--path` clones a fresh one (PyTorch is your step: the install is registered either way, and ComfyUI's own start error names the missing piece). - `update NAME` pins the core and each pack to a newer commit; `rollback NAME --component C` swaps back. A dirty component, or an install with jobs running, is refused: the update happens at the job boundary. - `remove NAME` drops the state entry; `--delete --yes` also removes the directory. The state lives in `engines.toml` beside `berth.toml`. Berth writes each install an `extra_model_paths.yaml` naming the node's model roots from `berth.toml`, so an install's models come from the same library the rest of the node uses; the daemon rewrites the file at startup, so a change to the roots applies on the next restart. --- ## Capabilities ### Leasing (the core) - **Explicit leases.** Engines start through `berth run`, which waits for a berth, starts the engine in its own process group, and gives the berth back when the engine exits. - **Priorities.** `foreground` > `interactive` > `batch`. An equal or higher request asks the holder to drain; a lower one waits and is refused with a reason naming the holder (exit 75), never an out-of-memory crash. - **Handoff in steps.** A drain tries the engine's own unload first (for llama-swap, its unload URL), then SIGTERM to the process group, then SIGKILL, each after a grace period. - **Measured release.** Berth grants the next engine only after the driver shows the old holder's processes gone, since an exited process can still hold memory. - **Stuck releases are caught.** A released lease whose memory never frees turns *aground* and keeps blocking, with a reason naming the process and how much it holds. - **A way out for a stuck release.** `berth reclaim [lease]` lists what the stuck lease recorded, PID, start time, memory and command, and anything on the card no lease recorded ("not Berth's", report only). With `--yes` it stops exactly the recorded ones, SIGTERM first and SIGKILL to the survivors after `--grace`, re-checking each PID and start time immediately before every signal. - **Process identity is PID plus start time**, so a reused PID never inherits a lease. - **Children stay on the lease.** Berth records every descendant of an engine's wrapper each tick, so a child that escapes its process group and reparents keeps the lease stuck under its own name instead of turning into a stowaway. - **Whole-card or sized leases.** `--needs-mib N` lets engines that fit share a card. - **Fail-open, never silent.** If the daemon is down, `berth run` still starts the engine but records it as an *unprotected run* that status shows (`--fail-closed` refuses). - **Survives a daemon restart.** A running engine stays up when berthd restarts or is upgraded; `berth run` dials the new daemon and re-attaches by PID plus start time. For 15 s after a start the daemon grants nothing new while such engines are still due back, so nothing is loaded onto a card an engine already holds. - **ComfyUI at a job boundary.** `--drain-comfyui` waits until ComfyUI's queue is empty before stopping it; a job in progress is never cut off. - **No juggling.** Two engines at the same priority drain each other: the last one asked for wins, which is what you want when you switch models. When two clients want different engines at once, that flips the card back and forth and every request fails. Berth calls it a juggle when an engine is drained within `juggle_window` (15 s) of getting the card while it is still busy (a request in flight, a ComfyUI job queued, a model loading). The engine ranking decides a juggle: the winner keeps or takes the card, and the loser waits for it instead of draining it back. An idle holder hands over at once, so chat, then an image, then chat again is three clean handoffs. ```toml [priority] order = ["llama-swap", "strata", "comfyui"] # first is best; omit to rank by use juggle_window = "15s" # a negative value turns it off ``` Without an `order`, the engine with the most hours on the card through Berth over the last 7 days ranks first (kept in `~/.local/state/berth/usage.json`); a tie leaves the holder in place. `berth run --group NAME` files a lease under an engine family: llama-swap runs each model under its own name, so give each `--group llama-swap`. `berth status` shows the ranking and a count of juggles stopped; the harbor log shows each one with the reason. - **A minimum turn per engine.** `min_turn = "5m"` on the engine entry (or `berth run --min-turn 5m`) gives the engine a turn it keeps for that long after the grant: in that time a request of equal or lower priority cannot drain it, and neither can a higher one, because a request interrupted halfway is a lost one.
