Only a hold (a game, a call, `berth hold`) takes the card out before the turn ends. ```toml [[engine]] name = "comfyui" min_turn = "5m" # the card stays this engine's for 5m after the grant ``` A blocked waiter is told how much of the turn is left ("next in line: comfyui has its minimum turn, 3m12s left"), and `berth status` shows the time a lease has left in the TURN column. When the turn ends the normal rules apply: a drain still starts at the slot or job boundary, and a minimum turn never cuts a request off. After a daemon restart, a re-attach starts a fresh turn. ### Games, apps and holds - **Claims cover work Berth does not start.** berthd scans the process table every 2 s. A *hold* claim keeps the card while its process runs: engines are drained and wait, with a 15 s linger so a launcher restarting the game does not bounce the card back. A *track* claim names an app's card memory so it counts against the card without being reported as a stowaway; nothing waits on it. - **Built-in pack, on by default.** Holds: Steam games (anything under Steam's `reaper`), Lutris and gamescope on Linux; Steam libraries (`steamapps\common`), Epic, GOG, EA, Ubisoft, Xbox and Battle.net games on Windows, with launchers, Wallpaper Engine and Lossless Scaling left out. Tracks: Blender, DaVinci Resolve, OBS, Kdenlive, Premiere, After Effects. `berth claims` shows every rule and what it matches now. - **Your own rules:** ```toml [[claim]] name = "training" cmdline = 'train\.py' # regex; on Windows it sees the exe's full path action = "hold" # or "track" linger = "30s" [claims] builtin = false # turn the built-in pack off ``` A rule can also match `exe` names (globs, `.exe` optional), a launcher `parent`, and exclude with `not_cmdline`. - **`berth hold [--for 2h] [--reason game]`** takes the card for you. It is a pinned lease at the top priority, so nothing drains it, and it ends on Ctrl-C, after `--for`, or when the process dies. - **`berth run --pinned`** gives an app a lease that is never drained (it keeps the card until it exits). - A hold cannot free memory held by something outside Berth: that memory is still reported, as contested. ### Models - **`berth pull hf:ORG/REPO[:QUANT|FILE|GLOB][@REV]`** resolves the revision to one commit, picks the GGUF for the quant (every part of a split model, and the vision projector when there is one), and downloads to `~/models///`. - **`berth pull civitai:VERSION_ID`** resolves a model version (or `civitai:model:MODEL_ID` for its latest, or the site's own URLs), downloads the files it lists to `~/models/civitai//`, and writes the same manifest. Public models need no key; gated files read `$CIVITAI_API_KEY`. - **`berth civitai search QUERY`** and **`berth civitai versions MODEL_ID`** find the ids a pull takes: models by name and asset kind, then a model's versions newest first. - **Integrity first.** Each file lands as `.part` and is moved into place only after its size and sha256 match the source's published hash. A mismatch deletes it and fails. - **Resumes.** Run the same command again after an interruption and it continues with a range request. A file already present and correct is skipped. - **The floor.** Before it downloads, a pull measures the destination root and refuses when its files would leave the root under `[library] free_floor` (a tenth by default, `0` turns it off). A root whose space this platform cannot measure says the floor was not checked, and goes on: a guard that cannot measure does not claim to guard. - **Shelves.** `berth models` reads each model for which shelf it is: chat, image, audio, or unshelved when the file states nothing. A root declared in `[library]` (say `shelf = "image"`) declares what it holds, and that beats a file's header. The SHELF column shows it, `--shelf image` lists one shelf, and the totals under the listing say how much of the library each shelf holds. - **The floor's view: `berth storage`.** Each root's filesystem (an ntfs3 root shared with Windows reads as ntfs3, on both sides of the share), the space it has left against its floor, what it can share (hard links, symlinks, reflinks), the other operating systems it is shared with, the shelves it holds, and when a berth last scanned it. A root under its floor fails the check. - **The in-root catalog.** A scan leaves `/.berth/catalog.json`: what it resolved, from which machine, and when. On a root two operating systems share, the second boot reads the first's resolutions instead of re-guessing them. The scan always recomputes; the file is a snapshot for the other side, never a cache this side trusts. - **`berth verify`** re-hashes pulled models against the manifest the pull wrote (`.berth-manifest.json`: source, name, ref, every hash), offline, and exits 1 on any change. - Gated and private models read `$HF_TOKEN` (Hugging Face) or `$CIVITAI_API_KEY` (CivitAI). - **`berth models`** reads every GGUF header (never the weights) in the tools' usual places and any `--dir` or `[models] dirs`. Split models list as one; vision projectors and MTP or draft heads list with the model they belong to (`--all` shows them on their own). `--usage 30d` adds requests and tokens per file from the harbor's request log, matched through llama-swap's config when that is how the model is served. - **The CACHED column.** How much of a model's files (its parts, and the vision projector and draft that go with it) sit in the kernel page cache, and the tier that share reads as: COOL at half or more, COLD below it. The check reads the kernel's page table (mincore), never a byte of a file, so it cannot pull a page in, and `--no-cache-check` skips it for a listing of a big library. The page cache is the kernel's: it keeps the pages until the machine needs the RAM, so the column says a restart is likely to read from memory, never that any RAM is held. - **`berth prefetch MODEL_OR_PATH`** asks the kernel to read a model's files into the page cache (posix_fadvise WILLNEED). The ask is made and the command returns at once; the kernel does the reading in the background, at its own pace, and takes the pages back whenever the machine needs the RAM. This is the manual form: while an engine that is about to run is still waiting for the card, its model's files can be warmed so the start reads from memory. The harbor's LIBRARY panel carries the same ask as a copy button on every model row. - **`berth models show NAME`** prints one model's header: architecture, context, tensor types, chat template, and what of the model sits in the page cache. - **`berth models export ollama NAME [--dry-run]`** writes a Modelfile and runs `ollama create`; a split model needs `llama-gguf-split --merge` first. ### Gateway (preview) - **One port for every engine.** `berth gateway` proxies OpenAI-style requests to the engine that serves the requested model, streaming. - **Cold starts under a lease.** An engine with `start` and `serves` in `berth.toml` starts on the first request that names one of its models, through the `berth run` path: lease, drain of the holder, measured release, then the start. One start per engine, however many requests arrive while it loads. - **Last switch wins.** Give gateway-started engines the priority of the engine they replace (`priority = "foreground"` next to a foreground llama-swap) and each side drains the other on demand. A lower priority waits behind the holder instead. - **Clear failures.** Unknown model: 404. A start the broker refuses or an engine that exits before it answers: 503 with the reason, the engine's own failure line, a `Retry-After` and an error `code` a client can branch on: `outranked` (lost a juggle), `drained_while_starting`, `no_berth`, `not_ready`, `start_failed`, `engine_oom` (the engine could not get the GPU memory it asked for), `no_headroom` (a cold start would leave the machine short of RAM, `--headroom-mib`) or `no_start`. An engine that crashes on start isn't started again on every retry: for 15 s, doubling to 5 min, the gateway answers at once with the same cause, and `Retry-After` says when the next start is allowed. A start that answers clears it. A model listed under `serves` by two engines fails `berth config check`. - **API key.** Bearer token on every route; `berth key` prints it (created on first use, mode 600). Loopback only; browser origins and non-loopback Host names are refused. #### Switch engines by naming a model Two engines that each want the whole card can't run together, and most harnesses can't start an engine before they call it. `berth gateway` starts it for them. Give an engine a `start` command and the model names it `serves` in `berth.toml`: ```toml [[engine]] name = "strata" type = "llamacpp" url = "http://127.0.0.1:8080" start = ["/path/to/strata/.venv/bin/python", "serve/server.py", "--engine", "strata", "--config", "strata-262k.json", "--port", "8080"] serves = ["router-strata", "qwen3.8-flash-next-iq2_xs"] priority = "foreground" # equal to the engine it replaces, so the last model you ask for wins ``` Run `berth gateway` (loopback `127.0.0.1:9799`; a user unit is in `contrib/berth-gateway.service`) and send your requests there with the node's API key as the bearer token. The gateway creates the key on first start (`~/.config/berth/api.key`, mode 600) and `berth key` prints it, so a client that runs commands for its key never has the secret written into its config: ```json { "baseUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:9799/v1", "apiKey": "!berth key" } ``` For each request the gateway: 1. reads the model name from the body; 2. hands the request straight to an engine that is up and lists that model (llama-swap and Ollama load their own models under their own leases); 3. otherwise starts the engine that `serves` it: as its own `berth run` process, under the same lease path (Berth drains the holder: llama-swap through its unload URL once its slots are idle, then SIGTERM, then SIGKILL), and the gateway waits until the new engine answers `/v1/models`; 4. proxies the request and streams tokens as the engine sends them. Requests that arrive during a start wait on that one start. A model no engine serves gets a 404, and a start the broker refuses comes back as a 503 with the broker's reason. A start waits for the card no longer than `--ready` (10 minutes); if the holder has not left by then, the request fails and the start is dropped, so it cannot take the card hours later. Asking llama-swap for one of its models later drains the gateway's engine the same way, so either side can take the card back. Measured on the reference RTX 4090 with an agent harness switching models between NInfer (through llama-swap) and Strata (262K context): | Switch | Drain of the holder | Request answered after | |---|---|---| | Strata on an empty card | none | 106 s (Strata's own cold load) | | Strata to NInfer | Strata released in 2 s | 41 s | | NInfer to Strata | NInfer released in 0.6 s | 110 s | At no point did the two engines hold the card at the same time. **A gateway restart keeps its engines.** Each engine runs as its own `berth run` process, in a systemd user scope on Linux (`systemd-run --user --scope`, when the user manager is reachable) so it is outside the gateway service's cgroup, else in a new session. The gateway writes each started run, with its PID, start time and lease, to a small file under the state directory (`~/.local/state/berth/gateway-engines.json`), and the run's own output goes to `~/.local/state/berth/engines/.log` (mode 600), never to a pipe the gateway holds, so a gateway that stops cannot break an engine's writes. While the gateway runs it copies the log to its own journal as well. When the gateway comes back it reads that file and adopts every engine whose process is still the same one, answering or still loading: the next request is proxied, not started again. Records for processes that left are dropped. Restarting during a 40-110 s cold start costs nothing but the restart itself. **Stopping the gateway keeps its engines too.** Each engine runs outside the gateway's cgroup (above), so stopping the gateway service does not stop the engines: they stay on the card under their own leases and keep answering. `berth stop ENGINE` is how one is stopped on purpose: the daemon asks the engine's leases to give the card back through the normal stop ladder, as when another engine asks for it, and a lease frees only after a card read shows the engine's memory gone. `berth stop ENGINE --wait` follows the daemon's event log until the leases are freed (exit 0) or stuck (exit 2, pointing at `berth reclaim` for the stuck ones). **Long waits and idle clients.** Cold starts take 41-110 s (table above), longer than many OpenAI clients wait before giving up. Streaming requests get the answer early: the gateway sends its SSE headers (`Content-Type: text/event-stream`, `Cache-Control: no-cache`) right away and writes an SSE comment every 10 s while the start runs, `: berth: loading strata, 34 s`, so proxies and clients keep the connection and a reader sees the wait moving. Once the engine answers, its body streams on; a start that fails sends one OpenAI-shaped error event with the same reason code the 503 path carries, then `data: [DONE]`. Non-streaming requests are unchanged; if a client drops a long non-streamed wait, raise its read timeout or make the request streamed. `GET /v1/berth/wait?model=NAME` blocks until the engine answers (a failed start is the same 503), so a harness can pre-warm before its first real request. The gateway serves `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions`, `/v1/embeddings` and a merged `/v1/models`, plus the ComfyUI surface: `POST /prompt` queues a workflow (starting ComfyUI under a lease when it is down, holding the request until its `/queue` answers), while `/ws`, `/queue`, `/history/`, `/view` and `/upload/` proxy to a running ComfyUI. Every route needs the key. The gateway listens on loopback only, refuses a Host that is not a loopback name (DNS rebinding) and refuses any request that carries a browser `Origin`, so a web page cannot start an engine. ComfyUI already hands off at a job boundary under a lease (`--drain-comfyui`); a drain first unloads its models via `POST /free`, and `--keep-comfyui-up` leaves the server on its port for OpenWebUI instead of stopping it. #### Open a stopped engine's web UI A bookmark to ComfyUI or Strata's chat page is a dead link while that engine is stopped. Give the engine a `gui` URL (where a browser reaches its web UI) next to its `start` command, and run the gateway with `--gui-listen 127.0.0.1:9796`: ```toml [[engine]] name = "comfyui" type = "comfyui" url = "http://127.0.0.1:8188" start = ["comfy", "--workspace", "/path/to/comfy", "launch", "--", "--listen", "127.0.0.1", "--port", "8188"] gui = "https://box.tailnet.ts.net:8188/" ``` Point the bookmark (or a home-page tile) at `http://127.0.0.1:9796/gui/comfyui` instead: - **ComfyUI answers:** the browser goes straight to its UI. - **ComfyUI is stopped:** the page says so and lists what holds the card (`llama-swap (NInfer-27B) active`), with a **Start** button. Opening the page takes nothing; only Start asks for the card. - **After Start:** the page says what the start waits for, in the broker's terms: "Waiting for strata release: finishing its current request", "Waiting for llama-swap (NInfer-27B) release: freeing its memory", then "loading comfyui". It opens the UI once ComfyUI answers. A failed start shows its reason code and a retry button. - `/gui/` lists every engine with a wake page. A start never runs two engines on the card at once. Berth drains the holder only at its boundary: llama-swap once its slots are idle (`drain_post`), ComfyUI once its queue is empty (`drain_comfyui`), and a server with no unload URL once its `/slots` show idle (`drain_slots`, below). A pinned holder (a game, a render, `berth hold`) is never stopped; the page says so and the start waits until it ends. The wake page needs no API key: it can only start an engine you gave both `start` and `gui`. It listens on loopback, accepts loopback Host names plus the gateway's `--allow-host` names (for `tailscale serve` in front), and takes a start only as a POST from its own page, so another site cannot make a visitor's browser drain the card. #### Drain a server at its request boundary An engine with `/slots` but no unload URL (Strata, a bare llama-server) would otherwise get SIGTERM mid-request when another engine asks for the card. `drain_slots` (or `berth run --drain-slots URL`) names its base URL: a drain waits until no slot reports `is_processing`, then stops it. ```toml [[engine]] name = "strata" type = "llamacpp" url = "http://127.0.0.1:8080" drain_slots = "http://127.0.0.1:8080" ``` The wait is unbounded by default, so a long generation is never cut off. `drain_max` (or `berth run --drain-max DURATION`, which wins) sets a ceiling on it: while the boundary is busy the wrapper prints a line each minute naming the slots and how long they have been busy, and once the ceiling passes it runs the normal stop ladder anyway and says so. With `--fail-closed`, it refuses the drain and keeps the child and lease instead. The same ceiling applies to a ComfyUI queue that will not empty. Fail-closed also rejects missing or malformed slot states and unreadable queue states. Without an explicit `drain_max`, slot checks and continuously unreadable ComfyUI queues refuse after four times the run's grace interval. A readable busy ComfyUI queue still waits without a deadline. A later drain can retry after the boundary recovers. The default fail-open policy and native parking path remain unchanged. #### End a ComfyUI session `exit_comfyui_idle = true` (or `--exit-comfyui-idle`) releases a run after its first completed job. Existing history does not count as new work. `exit_comfyui_idle_after` (or `--exit-comfyui-idle-after`) also releases a session that receives no work; zero leaves that wait without a deadline. These options require `drain_comfyui` and cannot combine with `keep_comfyui_up`. The session detector and daemon drains share one drain ticket. A refusal retains the original session deadline and work evidence, then retries after recovery. A readable busy queue is never treated as idle because history is unavailable. Completed-session release ends the process; daemon-requested parking and resume keep their native protocol and lease routing. Without these options, behavior is unchanged. #### Park in RAM (warm switch) A drain today ends with the engine's weights on disk, and the next request reloads them: tens of seconds every switch. Parking keeps the warm copy in host RAM instead: | Tier | Where the weights are | Switch back | RAM cost | |---|---|---|---| | hot | VRAM | now | none | | warm (parked) | host RAM, held by the engine | seconds | the footprint, committed while it lasts | | cool | the kernel page cache | load minus disk | nothing committed | | cold | disk | full cold start | none | Config, one line per engine plus the node's budget: ```toml [[engine]] name = "vllm-chat" type = "vllm" url = "http://127.0.0.1:8000" park = "hook" park_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8000/sleep?level=1" # optional: each beats the built-in resume_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8000/wake_up" [park] floor_gib = 4.0 # RAM a park must leave the machine (default 4) max_gib = 48 # cap on all parked copies together (default: no cap) ttl = "30m" # a parked copy is stopped after this long residual_max_gib = 2 # card memory a parked engine may keep ``` - **How it runs.** A drain first waits for the engine's boundary (idle slots, or an empty ComfyUI queue), then asks berthd to admit the park: admission measures the machine's available RAM, and a park that would leave less than the floor is refused quietly, so the drain runs as today. On admission the wrapper calls the engine's own offload hook and records the park; the lease stays parked, the card's residual counts, and a waiter builds beside it. The next request sends the resume, and the engine serves again in seconds. - **Adapters.** ComfyUI needs nothing: its unload keeps the models in RAM until memory pressure. vLLM needs `--enable-sleep-mode` and `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1` in the start command. SGLang needs `--enable-memory-saver --enable-weights-cpu-backup`. Any other engine can speak the park protocol (`contrib/PARK-PROTOCOL.md`): Berth probes `GET /berth/state` once and uses it when the endpoint answers. - **Eviction.** A parked copy is stopped, least recently parked first, when it passes its ttl, when the machine's available RAM falls under the floor, or one step at a time under memory pressure. Stopping a parked engine is a drain, and its run is Berth's own, so the stop is graceful. - **Who sits out.** llama.cpp and llama-swap have no offload call upstream yet, so they run today's drain; a park hook there waits for an upstream endpoint or a patched route. ### Visibility - **Stowaways:** every process holding VRAM without a lease, with memory, identity and first-seen time; optional desktop notification and webhook. Report-only by design. - **Contested grants:** a grant made while stowaways hold memory is flagged, not hidden. - **Event log:** every request, wait, drain, release, free, stuck lease, stowaway and probe change, with gap-free sequence numbers; `berth events -f` follows it live. - **The collisions board:** collisions avoided, VRAM handed off, drains, stuck releases caught, stowaways caught, contested grants, refusals. Each count links back to a recorded event. berthd keeps the board in `~/.local/state/berth/counters.json` (`--counters`), so a restart or a reboot carries the counts on. The harbor stores a reading a minute and its ticket counter shows the last 5 min, 15 min, hour, 24 h or 7 days next to the all-time board (`GET /v1/counters?range=5m|15m|1h|24h|7d`). - **The engines' estimated VRAM:** a run measures how much VRAM its leases held at their peak, and the broker keeps the last figure per engine in `~/.local/state/berth/footprint.json` (`--footprint`), across restarts. `berth status` shows it as EST. VRAM beside the engine's own figures, and the JSON names it `estimated_vram_bytes`. It is an estimate of what a run needs, never a reservation: a run that holds far more than the learned figure (1.5x, once the engine has three runs) logs an `engine.footprint` event, so a grown engine is seen instead of mis-sized. - **The queue in every wait reason:** every reason a waiter is sent starts with its place in the queue, "next in line" or "2nd in line (behind interactive comfyui)", so a client behind the head of the queue hears where it stands instead of silence. The waiting table of `berth status` shows the same place beside a start estimate, in seconds after the card frees: the measured starts in the waiter's chain, one per seat ahead plus its own. An unmeasured start says unmeasured and adds no number, and the holder's drain is never in the figure, because a request runs as long as it runs. - **Alerts:** one threshold table in `berth.toml` (`[alerts]`): warn and crit per key (`queue`, `ttft`, `tpot`, `p95`, `cache`, `reingest`, `vram`, `temp`, `power`, `kv`). The node evaluates it on its 5 s sample cycle, fires a desktop notification and webhook on entering a level, and logs `alert.raised` / `alert.cleared` events (`berth events -f`, the harbor log); a level stays until the value stays clear for `clear_polls` samples (default 3). GPU probe failure and aground leases are built-in danger alerts, always on. Default posture: no `[alerts]` table means no KPI alerts, and the notification channels are separately opt-in (`--notify`, `--webhook`). The harbor colors the same state the node notifies on: KPI tiles and GPU cells, a strip of the currently-breaching keys, and an overall LIVE / DEGRADED / OFFLINE state beside the connection pill. ### The harbor's views Everything the node collects shows in one of three tabs, and every panel answers a question an operator actually asks. **The CARD tab.** - **The ticket counter** answers "has anything collided?" with the collisions-avoided odometer, the seven collision tiles and the request KPIs, over the all-time board or a stored window. - **The tide** answers "who holds the card, and when?" with card memory by holder and the lease events overlaid, over a 1H / 6H / 24H / 7D / 30D picker. - **The model timeline** answers "when was each model loaded on each engine?" - **The departures board** answers "what is on the card right now?" with one row per lease: the ticket number, the engine, the class, the hold (measured once docked, asked-for while boarding, the parked engine's RAM copy while WARM), the state word, and the age. A WARM flag marks a parked engine; PARKING is the transitional state while the weights move to RAM. A boarding row carries a Q flag with its queue position and the node's completion estimate when the node sends them. Clicking a row opens the lease's ticket: the tier the weights live in (HOT on the card, WARM in RAM), the queue rows, the container a run is in, and the exact terminal order for the lease beside it as a copy button (`berth stop ENGINE`, `berth resume ENGINE`, `berth reclaim LEASE`). - **The berths, the machine, stowaways and no ticket** answer "what else is on the card and the host, and who holds memory without a ticket?" **The ENGINES tab.** - **The engine cards** answer "is this engine up and serving?" with the state the engine reports, its loaded models, decode and prefill rates, and its learned footprint as EST. VRAM: what its past runs measured, never "reserved". - **The library** answers "is this model warm?" with every model in the configured roots, each row showing shelf, quant, size, the CACHED share with its tier (COOL or COLD), the engine serving it when one reports it resident, that engine's EST. VRAM, and copy buttons for `berth prefetch NAME` and `berth models show NAME`. The listing is read-only here; the terminal does the acting. - **Card ranking, the KV pool, throughput, the token ledger, the leaderboard, the recent requests and context residency** answer the questions behind the request log, and the storage panel (advanced) says what the harbor's own store keeps. **The ABOUT tab** is this page's own documentation: the modes, the shortcut keys, and what every state word and figure means. ### Telemetry (built in, no other tool needed) - **GPU:** memory, utilisation, temperature, power against its limit, fan, SM and memory clocks, PCIe link, for **every card** in the machine with its real limits. - **Host:** CPU, RAM, swap, load. - **Engines:** every engine in the table above, found on its default port or configured on any other. Loaded models, decode and prefill tok/s, token totals, queue, draft acceptance, the context window per model (llama.cpp/NInfer `/props`, Strata `/health`, llama-swap per model proxy), and the live KV slot pool (`/slots`: per-slot context tokens against the window). An engine without those endpoints degrades to "no window / no slot data", never an error. An engine that was up and stops answering is shown as **unresponsive** (latched), distinct from one that never ran. - **Requests:** a 24-hour request log from llama-swap; requests per minute, p50 and p95 latency, prefill time, time per output token, cache and re-ingest share, a token ledger (1 h, 24 h, since start), a per-model leaderboard, and the most recent requests. - **History:** the node keeps the last hour at 5-second resolution in memory. The harbor stores it on disk (SQLite, no C toolchain needed): 1-minute rows for 30 days, per engine the KV pressure (peak slot fill against the window) and the resident models' windows, hourly rows for 400 days, and the request log for 30 days, de-duplicated by request id. Databases written before the KV column is added are migrated in place on the first open; nothing is ever rewritten. - **Model timeline:** when each model was loaded and unloaded on each engine, kept across restarts. A gap in the readings over 3 minutes is never drawn as loaded. - The UI labels engine-reported figures as the engine's own, apart from what the driver measures. ### Interfaces - **CLI:** one command tree with one output contract. `berth status`, `berth events -f`, `berth run`, `berth hold`, `berth stop`, `berth claims`, `berth pull`, `berth verify`, `berth models`, `berth gateway`, `berth wire llama-swap`, `berth engine check`, `berth config check`, `berth config show`, `berth export`, `berth key`, `berth skill install|show`, `berth update`, `berth version`, and for the node itself `berth daemon`, `berth harbor`, `berth service install|uninstall|status`, `berth reclaim`, `berth resume`, `berth prefetch`, `berth storage`, `berth civitai search|versions` and the ComfyUI suite under `berth engine install|show|update|rollback|remove`. Berth runs fully headless. ```sh berth wire llama-swap --config cfg.yaml # plan: which models lack a wrapper berth wire llama-swap --config cfg.yaml --write # apply; a backup stays beside the file berth wire llama-swap --config cfg.yaml --check # exit 1 when a model is unwired berth config check --strict # a warning fails the check, exit 1 berth config show --format toml # the evaluated config, ready to save berth engine check -v # what each engine reports, right now berth -q status; echo $? # exit codes only, for CI berth status --format json | jq .leases ``` Results go to stdout, diagnostics go to stderr. `--format` is `human` (the default), `json` or `yaml`, and `berth config show` also takes `toml`, the config's own file format. `-v` adds detail to the human view, and `-q` suppresses stdout and leaves the exit code as the answer. Exit codes are 0 (done), 1 (validation or logic: an invalid config, a warning under `--strict`, an engine that did not answer, a lease the broker refused) and 2 (berth could not do its job: unknown flag, missing file, berthd unreachable). `berth run` passes the engine's own status through and exits 75 when no berth was granted. Every read-only command changes nothing. - **Harbor web UI** (`berth harbor`): a departures board of every lease (the HOT / WARM tiers included: WARM marks a parked engine, with its parked RAM and age), a boat ticket per lease, the collisions counter, berths with measured memory, stowaways, the event log, and engine metrics. The tide (card memory by holder) and the model timeline share a 1H / 6H / 24H / 7D / 30D picker; the Engines tab adds the library (every model on the machine with its shelf, quant, size, cached tier, the engine serving it and that engine's EST. VRAM, with the terminal commands one row of copy buttons away), a queue KPI (the berth's own queue; each engine's own queue stays on its card), the KV pool (the live slots of each engine against their model windows, stored ranges the per-minute peak slot fill), context residency (the last requests' token figures against the model's window, plus the live KV sessions), a throughput chart, a 24H / 7D / 30D leaderboard and, in advanced mode, a storage panel. The top bar shows the overall state (LIVE / DEGRADED / OFFLINE) and a strip of the alerts currently breaching, colored from the node's own threshold state. Basic and advanced modes. While its update check is on and a newer release exists, the header shows it: the release, a link to it, and a button that copies `berth update`, the command that does the replacing. Read-only, strict content security policy. It listens on loopback by default (`127.0.0.1:9798`); passing a non-loopback `--listen` address (e.g. `0.0.0.0:9798`; a specific interface IP works too) is the explicit opt-in to expose it on your network: the startup logs a warning and the page shows a banner on every screen while exposed. There is no authentication in this release: expose it only on a network you trust; phones on that network get the full read-only dashboard. To reach it from elsewhere without exposing it, keep the loopback listener and put a same-machine reverse proxy in front (`tailscale serve`, caddy), passing the proxy's hostname with `--allow-host`. A systemd user unit is in `contrib/berth-harbor.service`. - **Prometheus** `/metrics` for Grafana and friends, on the `[metrics] listen` address. It serves loopback only and refuses a `Host` that is not a loopback name, so a web page cannot read it through DNS rebinding. The endpoint names your engines, leases and queue, so Berth never serves it off the machine. To scrape it from a Prometheus on another host, keep the endpoint as it is and either: - run a Prometheus agent or Grafana Alloy on the Berth machine, scrape `127.0.0.1`, and `remote_write` to your Prometheus; or - put Caddy or nginx on the same machine in front of it, sending a loopback `Host` (`header_up Host 127.0.0.1`, `proxy_set_header Host 127.0.0.1;`), with the proxy's own allowlist or auth on the network side. `tailscale serve` passes the tailnet name as `Host`, which `/metrics` refuses. - **Footprint:** the node uses about 0.2% of one CPU core and ~21 MB of memory on the reference box; the harbor about 0.4% and ~23 MB, writing to disk once a minute. --- ## Tested hardware The scenarios in [contrib/chaos](contrib/chaos/README.md) and the numbers below are how Berth's failure handling gets checked outside this tree. Run them on your card and add a row with the result, or report what happened with the [drain report issue form](https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth/issues/new?template=drain-report.yml) and the table credits you here. | GPU | VRAM | Driver | OS | Engines | Result | Tester | Date | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | RTX 4090 | 24 GB | 615.78.08 | Arch Linux | llama-swap + NInfer + Strata + ComfyUI | daily use | T-Crypt | 2026-10-20 | | RTX 4090 | 24 GB | 615.78.08 | Arch Linux | contrib/chaos scenarios 1, 2, 4 | pass | T-Crypt | 2026-10-20 | | RTX 4090 | 24 GB | 615.78.08 | Arch Linux | contrib/chaos scenario 3 (parent exits at once) | reported as a stowaway, never signalled: the known window | T-Crypt | 2026-10-20 | | RTX 5070 Ti + RTX 3060 | 16 GB + 12 GB | - | Windows 11 | the node, claims and the harbor, no engines | found [#81](https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth/issues/81) and [#82](https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth/issues/82) | mesquitafmr | 2026-10-21 | --- ## Swap numbers `contrib/bench/swap` through the gateway on the RTX 4090 workstation (driver 615.78.08, PCIe 4.0 x16), 2026-10-20: an opening request to A, then two cycles of B and A, a fixed prompt, greedy. | Engine | Cold first token | Warm first token (median) | Output identical | |---|---|---|---| | NInfer-Qwen3.8-27B (llama-swap) | 12.1 s | 16.1 s | yes | | Strata, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next UD-IQ4_XS | about 80 s to load | about 80 s to load | yes | Switching on every request is the ping-pong Berth's juggle guard exists to hold back: the switches to Strata waited behind the guard for llama-swap and measured 377-382 s end to end, of which the engine's own load (its log) was about 80 s. Park was off for both engines; parked resume numbers and `cuda-checkpoint` follow in v0.3.x. Run the bench on your card and add a row. --- ## Support matrix | Platform | Status | |---|---| | Linux + NVIDIA | Supported | | Windows 10/11 + NVIDIA | Experimental: leases, process attribution, job-object drains and game claims work, and the test suite runs on Windows in CI. Per-process VRAM comes from the GPU Process Memory counter (Task Manager's source), which also lists graphics apps and games nvidia-smi omits; host RAM and the page file come from GlobalMemoryStatusEx, and root space from GetDiskFreeSpaceEx. `berth service install` sets the node up as logon tasks; still no packaged installer and no locked-down control pipe. `contrib/windows/check.ps1` compares Berth's per-process VRAM with Task Manager's and writes a report for the drain report form. Known issues: [#81](https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth/issues/81), [#82](https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth/issues/82), both fixed in v0.3.2 | | AMD on Linux | Not supported yet; planned for v0.4 (a vendor-neutral probe, then amdgpu) | | Intel, Apple | Not supported yet | | Multiple GPUs | Inventoried with real limits; leases schedule one card per daemon today | --- ## Roadmap | Phase | What it delivers | Status | |---|---|---| | P0 | Safety core: identity, measured release, stuck and contested detection, unprotected runs | **Done** | | P1 | Node API: event log, collisions board, config, engine readers, `/metrics`, light probe | **Done** | | P2 | Harbor web UI; native telemetry, request KPIs, ledger, leaderboard, stored history, measured against Speculum parity | **Done** | | P3 | `berth hold` and claims for games and apps (**done**); drain and hold from the harbor, behind authentication (planned) | Partly done | | P3.5 | Node gateway: one OpenAI-compatible port; engines start on demand under a lease and drain each other | **Preview** | | P4 | Restart reconciliation: engines re-attach after a daemon restart, nothing left unprotected | **Done** | | P5 | Fleet: `berth install --harbor --join ` on every machine; nodes push metrics into the harbor's store (already built for one box in P2) | Planned | | P5.5 | Harbor router: one URL serves models from any node in the fleet | Planned | | P6 | ComfyUI job-boundary handoff on Linux (**done**); ComfyUI started on demand through the gateway (**done**); Windows node (**experimental**) | Partly done | | P7 | Offers: a waiting request can offer for an idle card on another machine; the holder decides | Planned | | P8 | Multi-GPU scheduling: a lease table per card, "any card that fits" | Planned | | P9 | Organisations: single sign-on, role-based access, audit log, Postgres, regional federation; a mobile app after | Planned | | P10 | Opt-in auto-yield: a card's owner can pre-approve offers for their own card | Later | ### Shipped: v0.3, fast swap and proof (2026-10-20) v0.3.0 went after the cost you feel most, a reload from disk on every switch, and after proof that Berth holds up when an engine misbehaves. It shipped park in RAM with adapters for ComfyUI, vLLM and SGLang and an open [park protocol](contrib/PARK-PROTOCOL.md); `berth stop`, `berth resume` and `berth reclaim`; engines in Docker and Podman; a place and an estimate in every wait reason; `berth update` and `berth service install`; the page-cache CACHED column and `berth prefetch`; per-process VRAM on Windows and the test suite on Windows in CI; and the proof kit: [contrib/chaos](contrib/chaos/README.md), [contrib/bench/swap](contrib/bench/swap), the drain report form and the [tested hardware](#tested-hardware) table. v0.3.1 fixed `berth update` answering from a stale cache. The [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md) has every entry. ### Next: v0.3.x v0.3.2 is a fix release. It carries the reports from the first Windows testers and the one feature merged since v0.3.1: - A minimum turn per engine (`min_turn`, `berth run --min-turn`), merged in [#80](https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth/pull/80). - The built-in Epic rule holds the card while only Epic's background services run ([#81](https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth/issues/81)). - Per-process VRAM on Windows can read past the card's size, because Berth sums every adapter ([#82](https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth/issues/82)). - `berth service install` now starts the tasks it creates on Windows and each writes a log, and the harbor and gateway take their listen addresses from berth.toml ([#89](https://github.com/T-Crypt/berth/issues/89)). After it, in v0.3.x releases. Each item has its building blocks merged or a spec written: - Cgroup attribution, which closes the one known stowaway window (chaos scenario 3: a child whose parent exits within one 2 s tick). - KV snapshots wired into the drain and start paths, so a sequence of agents skips the prefill after each switch. - Measured switch costs on the live daemon and the gateway (`/v1/berth/cost`, `/v1/berth/plan`). - Gateway fallback routing, and models started on demand for a standalone llama-server. - The gateway reads the next engine's files into the page cache while the holder drains; today `berth prefetch` does it by hand. - Parked resume numbers in [Swap numbers](#swap-numbers), which take the vLLM and SGLang park adapters out of experimental, and a measurement of NVIDIA's `cuda-checkpoint` for unmodified CUDA engines on Linux. Not started, and in no release yet: `berth fit` and scenes, so engines that fit together never swap. ### After v0.3.x | Release | What it brings | |---|---| | v0.4 | AMD on Linux, through a vendor-neutral probe; the Windows node out of experimental (a packaged installer, a locked-down control pipe) | | v0.5 | Multi-GPU scheduling, including one lease across two cards for engines that split a model | | v0.6 | The fleet: Berth on every machine, one harbor, one URL for every model | | later | Offers: a waiting request can ask for an idle card on another machine, and its holder decides | On hold: engine installers beyond the ComfyUI suite, the migration manager, and Berth swapping models itself. llama-swap already swaps models well. Berth works beside it, and a proposal to llama-swap for generic load hooks is planned, so Berth needs no wrapper line. ## What Berth never does - Kill a process it did not start, or any process by default. - Grant a card because a process exited, before the driver shows the memory free. - Claim memory is reserved when it is only estimated to be free. - Take a card from another user's machine without their consent (on one machine, only the priorities you set decide). - Require a cloud account, telemetry upload, or any other software to work. ## FAQ **What is an engine?** A program that runs a model on your GPU: llama.cpp, llama-swap, Ollama, vLLM, ComfyUI, a voice server. Berth doesn't run models; it decides which engine has the card. **Why not just llama-swap?** Use both. llama-swap swaps the models in its own config. Berth covers the whole card, including ComfyUI, games and the stray process holding memory that neither tool started. See [Berth and llama-swap](#berth-and-llama-swap). **Can a 700B model take turns on a 24 GB card?** No. Berth gives each engine the whole card in turn, or a sized share with `--needs-mib`; it doesn't make a model fit that doesn't. **How reliable is it?** Alpha. It runs every day on the author's RTX 4090 workstation, and v0.3 added `contrib/chaos`, the swap bench and the [tested hardware](#tested-hardware) table so you can check it on yours. **AMD? Windows?** AMD on Linux and a full Windows node are planned for v0.4. Windows with NVIDIA works today as experimental, and `contrib/windows/check.ps1` checks it on your machine; see the [support matrix](#support-matrix). **Can Berth handle ComfyUI on the host and vLLM in Docker?** Yes. Start each one under its own lease: `berth run --as comfyui -- python ...` for ComfyUI, and `berth run --as vllm --container vllm -- docker run --rm --name vllm --gpus all ... vllm/vllm-openai` for vLLM. The container's GPU processes are parented by containerd-shim, so the process tree cannot reach them; the lease names the container instead, Berth matches the processes by container ID, and the drain runs `docker stop -t 30 vllm` (podman's when podman resolved it) instead of signalling the wrapper. The handoff waits for the driver to show the container's memory gone, as with a host process. A container Berth did not start is still a stowaway: reported with its container ID, report only, never signalled. Details in [contrib/INTEGRATION.md](contrib/INTEGRATION.md). ## Contributing Issues and pull requests are welcome. [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) has the one command that proves a change (build, format, vet, tests, lint, as CI runs them) and the invariants a change must keep. ## License [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE). Copyright 2026 Trevin Tindall (T-Crypt), who created Berth and maintains it here. Forks are welcome: keep the [NOTICE](NOTICE) file and the copyright header in each source file, mark the files you change, and release your fork under its own name. The Berth name, the Pilot mascot and the artwork in `assets/` are not covered by the license. Third-party components: [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES).

items.name: hal0
items.description: Open-source self-hosted home AI inference platform for AMD Strix Halo — multi-backend slots, OpenAI-compatible gateway, Vue 3 + FastAPI + systemd.
items.readme_text:
### Open-source home AI inference platform **Stop running models from a chat tab.** [hal0.dev](https://hal0.dev) · [Install](https://hal0.dev/docs/getting-started/install/) · [Docs](https://hal0.dev/docs/) · [Benchmarks](https://hal0.dev/benchmarks) · [Roadmap](https://hal0.dev/#roadmap) · [Discord](https://discord.gg/7M4y6dcUyq)
--- hal0 turns a Linux box — ideally a Ryzen AI Max+ 395 with 128 GB of unified memory — into a private, OpenAI-compatible inference appliance. Chat, completions, embeddings, reranking, transcription, speech and image generation all answer on one `:8080/v1` surface, on hardware you own, with no per-token bill. Every inference workload runs as its own **podman container** under a `hal0-slot@.service` unit. `hal0-api` on `:8080` is the sole control plane — it owns slot state machines, dispatches `/v1/*` requests to the right slot port, and serves the dashboard. No shared inference daemon; no extra process to babysit. ```sh curl -fsSL https://hal0.dev/install.sh | sudo bash ``` > **v1.5.0 is the current stable release.** A minor release: new > functionality, no config-schema migration, and an ordinary `hal0 update` > from any 1.x box. Three changes can break a script or a setup: `hal0 update` > now restarts slots whose runner image changed and exits 2 while any still > run the old one; exposing a user-installed MCP server to Hermes or the > brain profile is refused until hal0 enforces its tool policy; and an > installed MCP server that would send its secrets over plain `http://` to > another host no longer loads. After > updating, re-run the installer once to pick up the new Hindsight limits, > the Open WebUI client key and the Hermes wrappers. Read the v1.4.0 > **Breaking** and **Migrations** notes in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) > first. The project has followed semver since v1.0.0; a minor release's > **Breaking** notes flag behaviour changes an operator or a script may > notice. Upgrades start at 1.3.0; on anything older, read > [Upgrading from an older release](#upgrading-from-an-older-release) first. > **⚡ The installer is the whole setup.** There is no separate first-run > wizard afterwards. `install.sh` asks where models should live, optionally > takes a HuggingFace token, seeds every capability slot, downloads the hal0 > brain steward model, and starts the API. When it finishes, open the > dashboard and assign models to slots. ## At a glance | | | |---|---| | **What it is** | One control plane, `hal0-api` on `:8080`, turning a Linux box into an OpenAI-compatible inference appliance — chat, embeddings, rerank, transcription, speech and image generation, each capability in its own podman container. | | **Install** | One `curl \| sudo bash` line. The installer probes hardware, seeds every capability slot, and starts the API — there is no separate setup wizard to run afterward. | | **Hardware** | First-class on AMD Strix Halo (ROCm iGPU + XDNA NPU); Vulkan and CPU fallbacks everywhere else, plus experimental CUDA. See [Hardware matrix](docs/reference/hardware-matrix.mdx). | | **Platform** | Linux + systemd + podman, including Proxmox LXC. macOS and Windows are not supported today — see [Support matrix](docs/reference/support-matrix.mdx). | | **Auth** | Enforcement is off by default (trusted-LAN posture) — opt in with `hal0 auth require on`. Once an admin key is configured, a LAN-bound box also gates mutating routes for off-box callers, even with enforcement off (v1.3.0). No TLS termination; front it with a reverse proxy if it's reachable beyond your LAN. | | **Chat UI** | OpenWebUI, prewired, on `:3001` — zero config. | | **Updates** | Cosign-signed tarball releases via `hal0 update`, with one-flag rollback. | ### If you know Ollama / llama.cpp / Open WebUI / LocalAI, hal0 adds… | You already know | hal0 adds | |---|---| | **Ollama** — pull a model, run it, hit one local API. | A dedicated slot per capability (chat, embed, rerank, STT, TTS, image) — each its own podman container with its own hardware backend, typed lifecycle, and per-slot logs, instead of one shared runtime doing everything. | | **llama.cpp** / `llama-server` — the inference engine itself. | hal0 runs llama.cpp *inside* systemd-supervised slots, with a state machine (`starting → warming → ready → …`), a model registry, automatic hardware-backend selection (ROCm/Vulkan/CUDA/CPU/NPU), and a benchmarking pipeline (`hal0 bench`) on top of it. | | **Open WebUI** — the chat frontend. | hal0 prewires OpenWebUI as the chat surface *and* is the backend it talks to — hardware probing, slot/model management, and a separate operator dashboard sit underneath, not just the chat window. | | **LocalAI** — an OpenAI-compatible gateway over multiple backends. | hal0 adds a live operator dashboard, a hardware probe that drives backend selection automatically, systemd-managed container lifecycle per slot, and a signed self-update path with rollback. | ## Screenshots

Dashboard — unified-memory hero, at-a-glance health, and live slot rows.
Slots — the inference engine: per-slot models, devices, and live telemetry.

Model registry — catalogue with quant chips and pull status.
Image generation — ComfyUI queue and GPU gauges.
Memory — Hindsight facts and graph extraction.

Services — Open WebUI, ComfyUI, Hermes, Hindsight, n8n with mDNS.
Stacks — declarative slot + profile + model bundles, applied atomically.
Settings — full hal0.toml parity with an Advanced section.
More in the docs.
## Install ### The one-liner ```sh curl -fsSL https://hal0.dev/install.sh | sudo bash ``` That fetches `installer/bootstrap.sh`, which needs `jq` and `cosign` on the box. It authenticates the channel manifest before parsing it, sha256- and Sigstore-bundle-verifies the release tarball, then hands off to [`installer/install.sh`](./installer/install.sh). Piped through `bash` it never prompts. Re-running it is safe: every provisioning step is idempotent and existing slot configs are never overwritten. Pick a channel with `HAL0_CHANNEL` (`stable` is the default; `preview` and `nightly` are the other two): ```sh curl -fsSL https://hal0.dev/install.sh | sudo HAL0_CHANNEL=preview bash ``` ### What the installer actually does 1. **Pre-flight** — systemd, Python 3.12–3.14, x86_64, a container runtime (podman preferred, auto-installed), GPU/NPU device visibility, disk space, free ports. 2. **Code + venv** — a versioned tree under `/usr/lib/hal0/` with a `current` symlink and a shared venv. 3. **Config** — `/etc/hal0/` with `hal0.toml`, `profiles.toml`, the ten curated slot seeds, and `api.env`. 4. **Hardware probe** — writes `/etc/hal0/hardware.json` and prints the detected backends. 5. **Brain steward model** — pulls the curated `lfm2.5-2.6b` (LiquidAI LFM2.5-2.6B-Q8_0, ~2.87 GB, 131k context) and binds it to the `brain` slot, so the dashboard's steward chat and its tool calls work out of the box. On an interactive terminal only, it then *offers* a larger agent model (15–31 GB, size printed first, default **No**). 6. **ComfyUI share** — creates the bind-mount directories the `img` slot needs and seeds custom nodes. 7. **Service start** — enables and starts `hal0-api` + `hal0.target`, the Hindsight memory engine, OpenWebUI on `:3001`, and the bundled Hermes agent. Full step list and the complete env-var table: [`installer/README.md`](./installer/README.md). ### Common install knobs | Variable / flag | Effect | |---|---| | `--models-dir=PATH` / `HAL0_MODELS_DIR=PATH` | Put model pulls somewhere other than `/var/lib/hal0/models` | | `HAL0_PORT=9090` | Bind the API somewhere other than `:8080` | | `HAL0_CHANNEL=preview` | Install from a channel other than `stable` | | `HAL0_NONINTERACTIVE=1` | Force flag/env defaults; never prompt, even on a TTY | | `HAL0_SKIP_SETUP=1` | Skip first-run seeding **and** both model steps | | `HAL0_SKIP_BRAIN_MODEL=1` | Keep the seeding, skip the brain pull (`brain` stays model-less) | | `HAL0_BRAIN_MODEL=` | Force a specific curated brain quant | | `HAL0_PULL_AGENT_MODEL=1` / `=0` | Opt in to the big agent pull unattended / force-skip it on a TTY | | `HAL0_PY_AUTOINSTALL=1` | Let the installer install a compatible `python3.12` | | `HAL0_SKIP_HINDSIGHT=1`, `HAL0_SKIP_OPENWEBUI=1`, `HAL0_SKIP_HERMES=1`, `HAL0_SKIP_COMFYUI=1` | Skip individual companion services | | `--no-start` | Provision everything, leave services stopped | | `--summary-json=PATH` | Write a versioned, machine-readable install summary (see [`installer/README.md`](./installer/README.md#--summary-jsonpath)) | ### Proxmox VE, one line On a Proxmox host: ```sh bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Hal0ai/hal0/main/scripts/proxmox-ve/hal0.sh)" ``` Creates an unprivileged Debian 13 LXC and runs the standard bootstrap inside it. `--advanced` opens whiptail prompts; every parameter has an env-var override (`CTID`, `RAM_MB`, `STORAGE`, …). Hardware-agnostic — Strix Halo passthrough still needs the privileged-LXC recipe. See [`scripts/proxmox-ve/README.md`](./scripts/proxmox-ve/README.md). ### Uninstall ```sh hal0 uninstall # prompts before deleting config + model data hal0 uninstall --keep-data # keep /etc/hal0 and /var/lib/hal0 ``` ## First ten minutes The dashboard is at `http://:8080`, the API at `http://:8080/v1`. Assign models from the dashboard, or from the shell: ```sh hal0 model pull / # resumable, disk-preflighted hal0 slot load agent --model # bind a model and start the container hal0 status # system + slot summary hal0 chat --brain # terminal REPL against the steward ``` Then point any OpenAI-compatible client at the box: ```sh curl http://:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hello"}]}' ``` `hal0 model pull` streams from Hugging Face into the model registry under the `user.*` namespace — a disk-space preflight fails fast before a multi-GB pull, and an interrupted pull resumes via HTTP `Range` instead of restarting from zero. ## What's new in 1.0 ### The whole platform is agent-reachable The admin MCP catalog went from 92 to **180 tools**: services lifecycle, ComfyUI, updater/doctor/health, hardware and request telemetry, the slots and models long-tail, bench, activity, approvals, runner images and NPU load/unload. The memory surface went from 5 tools to **26**, at feature parity with Hindsight 0.8.4 — including `memory_reflect` (LLM-backed synthesis), `memory_curate`/`memory_history` (the non-destructive "this is wrong" correction path), mental models, directives and async-operation polling. ### Slots start when you say so New `autoload` setting: binding a model no longer implies a boot start. New eviction `priority` (0–100) replaces the inert `lru = true` opt-in, so memory-pressure eviction actually works on a stock box — pressure and pre-load eviction unload the lowest-priority slot first, LRU as the tie-break within a tier, and `pinned` still exempts a slot entirely. ### Voice is a device-keyed switch Moonshine is back as the CPU STT engine in its own runner image. `cpu` runs Moonshine, `npu` runs whisper-v3:turbo, and a GPU device resolves to *no* STT engine instead of silently picking up a llama chat profile. ### Image Gen and Slots got their lifecycle right State-typed engine indicators, a Stop that drives the GPU arbiter back to inference mode, dropdown-driven runner image / binary selection (picking an image repopulates the binary dropdown with what that image actually ships), and a `GET /api/slots` that no longer multiplies `podman inspect` fan-out on wide boxes. ### Documentation moved into this repo `docs/` is the source of truth and publishes to hal0.dev through a mirror workflow, with a restored, v1.0-reconciled `getting-started/` section. ### Stability work that landed in the rc line - **Hermes bootstrap MCP wiring actually works.** The seed TOML never declared the builtin `[mcp.servers.*]` blocks, so the allow-list silently skipped wiring both servers, and the post-wire probe double-appended `/mcp` and 404ed. Bootstrap now also injects `HAL0_MCP_TOKEN` (0600) and renders `Authorization: Bearer` into the Hermes MCP client config when the box has auth on, refreshing it on `--repair` after a key rotation. - **ComfyUI `img` slot reliability.** Bind-mount dirs are created before spawn (a missing tree crash-looped podman with exit 125), readiness waits on ComfyUI's real `GET /system_stats` probe instead of 404-polling a llama-style `/health` for 180 s, and the fail-watcher no longer strikes a READY img slot to ERROR seconds after it comes up. - **`GET /api/slots` latency cut sharply on wide boxes** — no `podman inspect` for stopped slots, TTL-cached `podman image inspect`, and a single-flight 2 s snapshot that any slot mutation invalidates immediately. - **The Slots page no longer stalls on activity backfill** — the SSE stream takes a `limit` and the client coalesces frame bursts into one render per 50 ms. - **Brain tool calls no longer 500** with `Unknown (built-in) filter 'min'`. A corrected `hal0-brain-sft.jinja` ships bundled and the curated catalogue stamps it into the model's `chat_template` at pull time. - **A drifted hermes venv re-converges on upgrade** instead of staying broken. ### Quality-of-life - `hal0 doctor all` — one read-only pass over every surface with a rolled-up verdict and an exit code you can branch on. - `hal0 doctor bundle` — a redacted support bundle in one command. - `hal0 doctor ports --fix` — prune stale netavark DNAT rules that black-hole a port; it is the drill-down the `Slot ports` row used to lack. - `POST /api/profiles/generate` (`profile_generate` over MCP) drafts a profile from a registered model or a HuggingFace repo, with an optional `use_llm` pass that degrades to heuristics when inference is down. - Slot drawer: Profile moved under the model select (it rides the model choice); Runner Image is a catalog dropdown with a "Custom image ref…" escape hatch. - The `/mcp/memory` mount is now CLIENT-tier (was ADMIN), so memory-only agents no longer need the platform-admin key. Breaking changes, migrations and known issues for this release are in [`CHANGELOG.md`](./CHANGELOG.md). ## Why hal0 **Point your editor at your own box.** Aim any OpenAI-compatible client at `http://:8080/v1` — Claude Code, Cline, Continue, an SDK, a cron job. A dedicated `coder` slot can serve your editor while the `agent` slot serves chat, each on its own container, model and flag set. **Retrieval grounded on your data.** Embeddings and reranking are first-class slots, not an afterthought: `/v1/embeddings` and `/v1/rerank` run on the same box as chat, and the bundled Hindsight memory engine turns conversations into recallable facts behind an MCP server. **Speech and images on the same control plane.** Transcription (`/v1/audio/transcriptions`), speech (`/v1/audio/speech`) and image generation (`/v1/images/generations`, `/v1/images/edits`) are the same API, the same auth posture, the same dashboard — no second stack to operate. **Not another llama-server wrapper.** Every workload is a real systemd-managed slot with a typed lifecycle, persisted state (`/var/lib/hal0/slots//state.json`), SSE status streaming, per-slot journald logs and a GPU arbiter that keeps image generation from stealing the iGPU out from under a streaming completion. **Strix Halo native, but not Strix-Halo-only.** The probe is UMA-aware on Strix Halo and falls back to portable parsers (`/proc/cpuinfo`, `/proc/meminfo`, `lspci`) everywhere else. `platform` on `/api/hardware` resolves to one of `strix-halo`, `wsl2`, `lxc`, `proxmox-kvm`, `kvm`, `bare-metal-{nvidia,amd,intel}-gpu` or `bare-metal-cpu-only`, and the dashboard only labels memory "unified" when it actually is. Slot-fit warnings size against the real unified pool, not a BAR carve-out. **NPU multi-role via the FLM trio.** On Strix Halo with FastFlowLM installed, a single FLM process inside the `hal0-runner-flm` container hosts chat + transcription + embedding concurrently on one AMDXDNA hardware context — ~2 GB NPU memory, gemma3:1b at ~38.6 tok/s + Whisper-V3-Turbo + Embedding-Gemma all coresident. hal0 exposes this as one seeded `flm` slot (chat-first) whose `[npu]` table — or the dashboard's NPU drawer — toggles ASR and embed on the running `flm serve`. The host-side FLM `.deb` is installed for device-sanity probes only; inference runs in the container. See [docs/concepts/strix-halo.mdx](./docs/concepts/strix-halo.mdx). **An agent that lives on the box.** The hal0-brain steward drives the platform from the dashboard's top bar, and Hermes/Pi install as real services prewired to the local API and MCP servers. **Reliability bar.** Atomic env-file writes. Schema-validated TOML. Structured error envelopes (`{"error":{"code":"slot.not_ready",...}}`). Cosign-verified self-update with one-flag rollback. Priority-ordered concurrency with active-inference protection — a serving slot cannot be evicted out from under a streaming request. Privileged operations run through an allow-listed root seam, never a free-form shell. ## Benchmarks Numbers below are from the public leaderboard at [hal0.dev/benchmarks](https://hal0.dev/benchmarks) — 26 models measured end to end on the reference box (AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, Radeon 8060S iGPU, 128 GB LPDDR5X, ROCm 7.2.4), `rocm` lane, decode and prefill throughput plus TTFT, speculative accept rate, memory, watts and temperature per run. | Model | Params | Quant | Decode (tok/s) | Prefill (tok/s) | |---|---|---|---|---| | `qwen3.5-0.8b` | 0.8B | q4 | **169.8** | **6,248** | | `chadrock3-6-35b-uncensored` | 35B MoE | q4 | 102.1 | 890 | | `chadrock-35b-ace-saber` | 35B MoE | f16 | 100.5 | 903 | | `qwen3.6-35b-a3b-crown` | 35B MoE | f16 | 84.4 | 873 | | `qwopus3-5-4b-coder` | 4B | q4 | 85.0 | 889 | | `qwen3-4b` | 4B | q4 | 61.9 | 1,849 | | `gemma-4-26b-a4b` | 26B MoE | q4 | 40.9 | 1,336 | Concurrency and non-LLM lanes, same box: | Workload | Measurement | |---|---| | Chat + embed, concurrent | ~258 tok/s aggregate | | NPU chat (FLM trio, gemma3:1b) | ~38.6 tok/s in ~2 GB NPU memory | | TTS — Kokoro (CPU) | ~0.18 real-time factor | | TTS — Qwen3-TTS (ROCm) | ~0.48 real-time factor (~2.1× realtime) | Benchmarking is a first-class subsystem, not a spreadsheet: `hal0 bench plan|run|results|eval|bundle|upload` drives `llama-bench`/`llama-server` under a record schema with a dedup identity key, an in-dashboard Benchmarks page (roster / runs / evals / run-queue), and regression journaling. See [docs/reference/model-roster-benchmark.mdx](./docs/reference/model-roster-benchmark.mdx). ## What's in the box - **OpenAI-compatible `/v1/*` API** — chat, completions, embeddings, rerank, audio transcriptions, audio speech, image generations, image edits, models. Drop-in for any OpenAI SDK; point your client at `http://localhost:8080/v1` and go. - **Slots** — each named target carries a `type` (`llm | embedding | reranking | transcription | tts | image`), a `device` (`gpu-rocm | gpu-vulkan | gpu-cuda | cpu | npu`), a `model`, plus `autoload`, an eviction `priority` and an optional `default`. Ten curated slots (`agent`, `brain`, `coder`, `embed`, `flm`, `img`, `qwen3tts`, `rerank`, `tts`, `utility`) are seeded into `/etc/hal0/slots/.toml` on install and each gates on its own runtime validation at load time — the `flm` NPU slot simply stays grey without FastFlowLM hardware. Add your own with `hal0 slot create NAME --type TYPE --model MODEL`. A deliberate `hal0 slot delete` is tombstoned, so re-running the installer never resurrects it. - **Model owns its tune** — since v1.0 the *model*, not the slot, owns `context_size`, `extra_args`, `chat_template`, `profile` and MTP. A slot's `[model].context_size` is a ceiling; a model with no stamped tune inherits its profile's template as a floor. - **Container runtime** — every slot runs as its own podman container under `hal0-slot@.service`, bound to a loopback port (8081–8099 + fixed seeds). `hal0-api` on `:8080` is the only control plane. See [docs/concepts/architecture.mdx](./docs/concepts/architecture.mdx). - **Hardware-aware probe** — detects GPU / NPU / unified memory, writes `/etc/hal0/hardware.json`, and surfaces VRAM/RAM fit warnings inline in the slot form and during install. - **Dispatcher** — registry-aware routing, single-flight, cold-cache prefetch, and upstream fallback (OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google AI Studio, Ollama, custom OpenAI-shaped endpoints). Mix local + remote per-model in one config. - **Dashboard** — React 18 + Vite UI for slot/model management, hardware-aware configuration, live logs, system health and a built-in chat page (popout window + reasoning toggle). SSE-backed status and log tail; a Journal panel streams per-slot container logs from journald. Live telemetry — Power & Thermal (GPU clock/temp/power) and per-slot throughput — is on by default. The slots page splits into Inference | Image Gen tabs; the Image-Gen tab operates the ComfyUI container (live GTT/RAM gauges, queue depth, model inventory) with a gated inference ⇄ generation iGPU switchover behind a blast-radius confirm. - **AI Capabilities page** — one settings surface for TTS, STT, embeddings, reranking, image generation and the NPU, with per-panel probe-failure surfacing instead of a silent grey Save. - **Stacks** — declarative, runtime-switchable model/slot layouts. A `StackConfig` is planned into a change set, applied atomically (with rollback) and converged against the live slot set; drift is detected by content hash. Stacks export/import via a checksummed `.hal0stack.json` envelope, and a live config can be snapshotted back into a Stack. - **OmniRouter (8 tools)** — `generate_image`, `edit_image`, `text_to_speech`, `transcribe_audio`, `analyze_image` (vision), `embed_text`, `rerank_documents`, `route_to_chat`. Dispatched client-side from any chat slot whose model carries the `tool-calling` label, and filtered per request — a tool only appears in the prompt if its target slot is enabled and its model carries the required labels. - **Companion-service management** — `/api/services` is the declarative source of truth for OpenWebUI, Hermes, Hindsight, ComfyUI and n8n: audit-logged systemd lifecycle actions (start/stop/restart/enable/ disable), mDNS `.local` advertisement, and a dedicated Services page. OpenWebUI is prewired at `:3001` with zero config. - **Image generation, day one** — `POST /v1/images/generations` via ComfyUI in the `img` slot container (ROCm). The installer seeds the `img` slot and its ComfyUI model share. - **Atomic self-update with rollback** — `hal0 update --channel stable|preview|nightly`. Cosign-verified tarballs swap a `/usr/lib/hal0/current` symlink; `--rollback` reverts. Staging happens in a root-only directory with the authenticated digest pinned to the very file object the archive is extracted from. ### Agents, MCP, and the brain steward hal0 ships **two MCP servers** and **two bundled agents**. The MCP servers (`/mcp/admin` for slot / model / capability / config / hardware / log admin, `/mcp/memory` for Hindsight-backed long-term memory) are reachable by any MCP-speaking client — Claude Code, RAG services, your own scripts. `/mcp/admin` is ADMIN-tier; `/mcp/memory` is CLIENT-tier as of 1.0, so a memory-only agent does not need the platform-admin key. Both bundled agents can be installed simultaneously: `pi-coder` (CLI shape, from the `Hal0ai/pi-mono` fork via `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` on npm) and `Hermes-Agent` (service shape, via the hal0-owned `hermes` wrapper — `hal0-hermes` remains a back-compat symlink — connecting to `hal0-api` at `HAL0_INFERENCE_BASE=http://127.0.0.1:8080`). Install either with `hal0 agent install `. Destructive MCP calls (`model_pull`, `slot_delete`, `config_write`, …) gate through a header bell + inbox modal in the dashboard, with CLI parity via `hal0 agent approvals {list,approve,deny}`. The **hal0-brain steward** is a third, built-in persona wired to the dashboard's top-bar agent chat — no install step. It drives the platform through the **180-tool `hal0-admin` catalog** (models, slots, stacks, profiles, settings, upstreams, benchmarks) under a **per-persona tool policy**: `tools_allowed` hides tools, `require_approval` tightens them, and a `POLICY_NO_LOOSEN` floor keeps destructive and secret-bearing tools (`*_delete`, `config_write`, `provider_credential_write`) always gated — no persona edit can disarm them. Gated calls **pause the turn** for inline approve/deny. A `[brain_chat]` config gives operators a hard kill switch, a read-only mode, loop-budget knobs and a slot override (run the steward on any slot, e.g. `hal0/npu`) from **Settings → Agents / Brain**. The seeded brain model is a native tool-caller, so the steward executes its own calls on the `brain` slot out of the box. Binding a larger model to the `agent` slot is the optional upgrade path: `[brain_chat] tool_model` (default `hal0/agent`) runs tool rounds there while chat stays on the brain slot, so a runner that cannot emit parseable tool calls reroutes instead of failing the turn. Set it to `off`, `none` or `disabled` to route tool turns nowhere. See [docs/concepts/agents.mdx](./docs/concepts/agents.mdx), [docs/reference/mcp-tools.mdx](./docs/reference/mcp-tools.mdx) and [docs/guides/run-agents.mdx](./docs/guides/run-agents.mdx). ## Backends Each capability runs in its own container, supervised by `hal0-slot@.service`. Two things compose to launch a slot: the **runner image** (slot-owned — `binary` plus the optional `image_pin`; each runner's image is pinned in `manifest.json`) supplies the engine, and the **profile** in the catalog supplies the bench-tuned flag bundle. Profiles are device-agnostic tune templates; they no longer carry an image. | Capability | Runner (binary) | Device | Profile | |---|---|---|---| | chat | `standard` (`llama-server`) | `gpu-rocm`, `gpu-vulkan` | `chat`, `chat-long-context`, `dense`, `moe`, `thinking`, `coding`, `brain` | | chat (NVIDIA, experimental) | `cuda` (`llama-server`) | `gpu-cuda` | `chat` | | chat (fallback) | `cpu` (`llama-server`) | `cpu` | `cpu-chat` | | embeddings / rerank | `standard` (`llama-server`) | `gpu-rocm`, `gpu-vulkan` | `embedding`, `reranking` | | chat + STT + embed (NPU) | `flm` | `npu` | `flm` | | transcription | `moonshine` / the FLM trio above | `cpu` / `npu` | `moonshine` / `flm` | | TTS | `kokoro` / `qwen3tts` | `cpu` / `gpu-rocm` | `kokoro` / `qwen3-tts` | | image | `comfyui` | `gpu-rocm` | `comfyui` | A device also has a *default* profile it resolves to when a slot names none — `gpu-rocm`, `gpu-vulkan` and `gpu-cuda` resolve to `chat`, `cpu` to `cpu-chat`, `npu` to `flm`. The seeded slots override that where it matters: `agent` ships on `dense`, `coder` on `coding`, `brain` on `brain`, `utility` on `chat`. The seeded profile catalog is virtual — it lives in code (`SEED_PROFILES`) and is overlaid on every load, so a re-tuned seed reaches every install on upgrade instead of being frozen by a stale on-disk copy. `/etc/hal0/profiles.toml` is for *your* profiles: `chat`, `chat-long-context`, `dense`, `moe`, `thinking`, `coding`, `brain`, `embedding`, `reranking`, `cpu-chat`, `flm`, `kokoro`, `moonshine`, `qwen3-tts` and `comfyui` are immutable seeds you clone under a new name to customize. `voice.stt` switches Moonshine (CPU) ⇄ FLM's whisper-v3:turbo (NPU) and `voice.tts` switches Kokoro (CPU) ⇄ Qwen3-TTS (GPU) without reconfiguring the slot. There is no GPU STT engine — a GPU device resolves to none rather than silently borrowing a chat profile. Every seeded chat profile requests `-fa auto`, so Flash Attention is probed at startup and falls back cleanly when it cannot be scheduled on its layer's device. A model with a measured win from forcing it can set `-fa on` in its own `defaults.extra_args`. The NPU path is opt-in: the installer places a FastFlowLM `.deb` on the host (SHA-pinned per distro — Ubuntu 24.04/25.10/26.04 and Debian 13) for device-sanity probes (`flm validate`); inference runs inside the `hal0-runner-flm` container. With FLM present the installer seeds the `flm` slot, and the NPU trio activates once `flm validate` passes.
