items.title: Tessl 团队分享：不再逐行审查 AI 生成代码，改为验证意图
items.summary: Tessl 工程师 Ankit Jain 分享团队 PR 量翻四倍、代码几乎全部由 AI 生成后，放弃逐行 diff 审查、改为在代码生成前审查意图并逐条验证验收标准的做法。关键实践包括维护 offer-skill 技能理解代码变更，以及把重复出现最多的审查评论固化成机器自动执行的不变量规则，作者预计第二个月起审查负担明显缩小。
items.original_text: By Ankit Jain, for AI Native DevCon What do you do when your team merges four times more pull requests than it did a year ago, and almost none of that code was typed by a human? That's where my team is today. Almost everything we ship is AI-generated and human-assisted, and the volume keeps climbing. We did the obvious thing first. We tried to scale code review by using AI review tools or adding stricter checklists. None of it worked. What worked was giving up reading code line-by-line entirely and building a verification layer around intent. Why scaling code review for AI-generated code didn't work Earlier this year I wrote How to Kill the Code Review for Latent Space. It went viral, and I haven't stopped talking about the AI code review bottleneck since. The problem keeps coming up because its cause isn't going away. At four times the volume, review became the slowest step in shipping. Most teams that use AI coding tools run into the code review bottleneck and try to solve it with some combination of more reviewers, adding AI code review tools, or stricter rules for code generation. But the real problem is what's being reviewed. A diff tells you what changed, but it doesn't tell you what the change was supposed to do. This post covers the two practices that made the most significant difference for us, and the framework they ended up fitting into. As a baseline, we now maintain a shared skill that we call "offer-skill," named after our engineer who started it. It turned into the skill that everyone uses to understand the code change. Review the intent, not the diff The conventional wisdom says human judgment belongs at the end. Someone reads the code and decides whether it looks right. With AI-generated code, that puts the reviewer in a bad spot. They read 400 lines and try to reverse-engineer what the change was meant to do. The ticket description only helps if there is a team discipline of maintaining good tickets. The reality is that most tickets are poorly drafted, and the actual intent and behavior drift from the ticket. So we moved human judgment to the front. Before a single line is generated, we review the intent: the acceptance criteria, the constraints, and the edge cases. That's where a senior engineer's attention is worth the most, because a wrong idea costs almost nothing to fix at that point. Then we treat that intent as a contract we can verify. Each criterion gets a deterministic verdict, with evidence attached. A review looks different now. The reviewer isn't scrolling through a 500-line AI-generated diff. They're looking at five criteria verdicts, with screenshots and request traces that show what happened. What does this mean for devs? The author and the reviewer both know what the code is supposed to do before it's merged. And if you can't say what a change should do before it exists, reading it afterward won't tell you. Every team has standards that live in senior engineers' heads. They get enforced one review comment at a time. Look through your review history, and you'll see the same comments written over and over. Those are team standards hiding in plain text. At four times the PR volume, repeating them by hand becomes a bottleneck of its own. So we went back through X our recurring review comments and turned them into invariants: reusable rules that a machine enforces on every change. A good invariant is boring and specific. For example: Use the Money type for anything with a currency. No direct writes to the users table. Structured logger only, no print statements. Not every comment qualifies. If you want to try this, start with your last 1,000 review comments. The 20 you repeat most are your first invariants. You aren't inventing rules. You're writing down the ones you already have. Once a standard is an invariant, nobody has to flag it again. Have in mind that the transition will not happen overnight. Month one will most likely feel like the team is doing double work: reviewing code and building invariants. Set clear expectations with the team: the register takes time to build. During month two, the register catches enough that reviews shrink. In month three, the reviewer reads intent, not code. Code review didn't disappear, it changed shape We still review. What changed is what the review is for. The two practices above are part of a five-step shape I now use to describe it: Argue. Let agents challenge each other's solutions before the pull request exists, when changing course is cheapest. Capture. Record the intent and acceptance criteria, and put them on the pull request. Codify. Turn the comments your team keeps repeating into invariants. Debate. Spend human review time on the decisions, not the diff. Own. Decide who owns the rules that verify the code. For us, the result is that code review is no longer the bottleneck. Senior engineers stopped reading 500-line AI-generated diffs. tl;dr Scaling diff review to match AI output doesn't work. Review the intent before the code is generated, and verify each criterion with evidence. Turn your recurring review comments into invariants. Keep humans on the decisions and on ownership of the rules. When AI writes most of your code, a human's review is best spent on what the change should do. I'll walk through the full workflow at AI Native DevCon, with live examples of invariant definitions and before/after metrics.

items.title: Modal 推出 Sticky Sessions：同一会话请求始终路由到同一容器
items.summary: Modal 发布 Sticky Sessions，基于 Modal Servers 让同一会话的所有请求固定路由到同一容器，用 @modal.sessioned() 装饰器配合 SDK 或 HTTP API 即可创建。
items.original_text: At Modal, our serverless compute powers real-time inference, training, and batch jobs, scaling automatically with demand. Sandboxes offer a different model, containers whose lifecycles you explicitly control. A growing number of workloads require something in-between; autoscaling serverless compute that maintains continuity between requests. Consider a speech-to-text model with decoder state for an audio stream, a voice agent that holds a conversation, or a multiplayer game . For these workloads, users must come back to the same container on every reconnect for the entirety of their session. We recently launched Sticky Sessions , built on top of our low-latency Modal Servers . Every sessionâs requests land on the same container. To use Sticky Sessions, just create a Modal Server with the @modal.sessioned() decorator and start the sessions with the SDK or the HTTP API : Serverless with strong affinity Modal has supported WebSockets via Web Functions for some time. However, a WebSocket connection is tied to a Function âinputâ, not a containerâif the connection drops, a new input is created on reconnect and can land on a different container. Stateful web UIs such as Gradio and Streamlit are workloads that need strong affinity guarantees between requests and backend containers. Every request has to reach the process that holds the userâs state. One anti-pattern workaround is setting max_containers=1 , which guarantees stickiness by giving up scaling entirely. Modal Servers already provide a softer form of affinity ; requests that share the same Modal-Affinity-Routing-Key header are routed to the same container in a best-effort manner. The container can still be scaled down or replaced at any time, routing future requests to a different container. Sticky Sessions provide stronger routing guarantees by ensuring all requests in the same session land on the same container. Modal Servers gave us the foundation Sticky Sessions build on the infrastructure we developed for Modal Servers . At the core of this infrastructure is our in-house stateless proxy (fprs). The proxy provides low-latency routing and load balancing using in-memory cached routing state reconciled from durable storage. Servers already give us a way to route HTTP traffic to a container, manage container lifecycles, and scale the fleet based on demand. Sticky Sessions needed three things that the current request-level routing didnât provide: Fixed routing: Every request in a session reaches the same container. Session lifecycle: The containerâs host tracks which requests belong to which sessions and determines when each session becomes idle. Session-based autoscaling: The container fleet scales with the number of active sessions rather than requests. Making serverless infrastructure session-aware From the clientâs perspective, a Sticky Session works like a pipe. Once the client creates a session, every future request for that session will be directed to the same container. This may seem simple, but Modalâs serverless infrastructure was built and optimized for the opposite idea; that individual requests are independent. In viewing Modal Servers from the perspective of sessions (rather than just requests), we had to reason about authorization, load balancing, and autoscaling from first principles. Authorization Modal Servers require Proxy Tokens by default. To share Sticky Sessions, you shouldnât need to turn off authentication or pass your Proxy Token around. Instead, each sessions.start() request returns a signed session token to grant access to that session. Sharing this token among clients lets multiple participants access the same state in a room, game, or collaborative app. Maintaining the session-to-container mapping in the proxy would require keeping that mapping consistent through restarts and across multiple replicas. To avoid this, we encode routing metadata directly into the token. Our proxies validate the token and route requests to the container holding the session. Load Balancing Since weâre not storing session state in the proxy, the authoritative view of session state lives only on the host that owns the session. This means the load balancer cannot have an instantaneous global view of available capacity. To discover available capacity, our load balancers periodically probe containers for a snapshot of their available concurrency. The load balancers then use a combination of recent routing decisions and the probed snapshots to inform container selection. This evenly distributes sessions across available containers while minimizing wasted roundtrips to containers that are out of capacity. Autoscaling Modal Servers autoscale on request volume, aiming to achieve a per-container request concurrency target. The request-driven autoscaler assumes that request traffic can be rebalanced evenly across the serving fleet of containers. This model works well for stateless Servers. However, Sticky Sessions behave differently in that session traffic is not movable . Each sessionâs traffic has to land on the same container even if traffic volume varies across sessions. This motivated having sessions be the unit of concurrency, akin to Modal Functions with inputs. A container can be configured to run 1 or more sessions concurrently. When concurrency runs out, new sessions wait in a queue for existing sessions to end or a new container to become ready. The autoscaler continuously monitors active session counts and queued demand to make scaling decisions that appropriately size the compute fleet. What Sticky Sessions unlock Sticky Sessionsâ strong routing and lifecycle guarantees on top of Servers enable first-class support for a new suite of applications on Modal: Low-latency voice agents: The Modal Phonon Voice Bot runs a Pipecat agent with Gradium Phonon text-to-speech over WebRTC. Each call is a Sticky Session that is pinned to a container, so WebRTC signaling reaches the container that holds the peer connection. The session keeps the container active while the audio flows through WebRTC. Shared rooms : Our sessioned chat room example backs each chat room with a Sticky Session. Every client that connects with the session token is routed to the same container. Each roomâs messages are broadcasted to everyone in the room. Clients can drop and reconnect to the same room for the lifetime of the chat room session. Gaming: Gaming applications keep state in memory to maintain continuity and reduce lag. Sticky Sessions support both preserving progress and hosting concurrent rooms of players. A brave, sticky world At Modal, we love using Modal. Amidst our quest for infinite scale and frontier performance , we find ourselves playing (a lot of) Curvytron . And of course, we host our own speedy (no more input lag excuses!) us-east deployment on Modal Servers atop Sticky Sessions. Like many multiplayer games, Curvytron has players in a shared room competing against one another in real-time. With Sticky Sessions, players can create a room, share the game link, and play with others! Modal scales based on active room count automatically. Try it out here! Special thanks to Claudia Zhu, Richard Gong, Akshat Bubna, Michael Waskom, and Ben Shababo for helping shape this feature! If youâre interested in building foundational infrastructure for the next generation of software, weâre hiring .

items.title: Anthropic 用 Claude 设计出针对蝎子神经毒素的蛋白质迷你结合剂
items.summary: Anthropic 让内部研究模型在 Claude Science 中主要自主运行 64 小时，设计针对五种蝎子神经毒素的蛋白质迷你结合剂，共生成 318,484 个设计、筛选出 180 个。
items.original_text: Summary: As part of our work experimenting with how Claude can help accelerate drug discovery, we asked an internal research model to design minibinders (small proteins that attach tightly to a target) against scorpion neurotoxins. Claude worked from our prompt and four follow-ups, which we developed in collaboration with the financial investment research firm Citrini Research. Teams at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience experimentally tested 211 designs for binding. Of these, 17 met our criteria. We’re releasing all 211 designs and their data as a resource for the field. In August, we showed how Claude designed protein minibinders after being given a single prompt. A month before we released those results, a team from Citrini Research had approached us with an interesting question: could Claude (and AI drug discovery more generally) enable a group of motivated nonexperts to tackle a genuine problem in human health? Members of our life science research team set out to answer this, first by brainstorming problems with Claude. We landed on asking for Claude’s help designing novel protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins, with the hope that they could one day be used to develop a scorpion antivenom. Scorpions sting 1.2 million people or more every year, resulting in more than 3,250 deaths, mostly among children in parts of the world with limited access to medical care. New treatments are expensive to make, and are also unlikely to earn back the cost of developing them. With so little investment, scorpion envenomation has been described as a neglected tropical disease. We started by giving Claude the same prompt we’d used in our earlier protein-binder study, after modifying it with Citrini. 1 Over the next 64 hours, an internal research model, operating within Claude Science, worked mainly autonomously, although we directed its work with four follow-ups. Under our supervision, Claude analyzed the research data, generated the figures, and drafted the final report. Claude’s design campaign produced 17 protein binders that each bind to one of four scorpion neurotoxins that are known to be dangerous to humans. Throughout the process, Claude generated 318,484 protein designs and selected 180 of them for testing. Our team added 31 more, with Claude’s help. Our partners at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, two contract research organizations (CROs), lab-tested all 211 designs to see if they would bind to the toxins they were designed against, and 17 designs met our criteria for a binder. We have not confirmed whether these binders neutralize scorpion venom in a cellular environment, so we do not claim to have produced an antivenom. We sent Claude’s work to two outside experts, Susana Vázquez Torres and Timothy P. Jenkins, who said they felt this work was a promising first step. If AI can now design credible binders against several hard-to-target toxins in days and they can be confirmed in the lab within weeks, this could, in theory, speed up discovery for envenomation and other neglected diseases. The challenge, as always, is turning those binders into safe, affordable, and widely accessible drugs. We share more detail in our technical report , and are making all 211 designs and their data available . Designing a binder against almost any target no longer seems unrealistic. We can now obtain very tight binders remarkably quickly, and binding itself is no longer the main bottleneck. For venomous animals such as snakes and scorpions, whose bites and stings kill or seriously injure large numbers of people, particularly in underserved regions, the real impact will come from tackling the parts of the therapeutic pipeline that go beyond binding. The challenge is to use these extraordinary tools to develop molecules that can become real drugs, ones that are safe, affordable, and widely accessible. Susana Vázquez Torres , Postdoctoral Researcher, Structural Biology Programme, Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO), Madrid, Spain. Designing de novo binders against five toxins from four species of scorpions Scorpion venom contains multiple protein neurotoxins. The neurotoxins that are most likely to harm or kill humans attach to sodium channels , large proteins embedded in the membranes of nerve cells that allow them to fire. When sodium channels are disrupted, nerves fire at the wrong time—this releases large amounts of stress chemicals, like adrenaline. In severe cases, this can cause heart failure and excess fluid buildup in the lungs, occasionally resulting in death. There are some antivenoms available for scorpion stings. They’re generally made using the antibodies of immunized animals, a process that can take months. Venom is milked from thousands of scorpions and used to immunize horses; scientists then purify the resulting antibodies from the horses’ blood. Traditional antivenoms can work when given early, but they’re usually effective for only a small number of neurotoxins. They’re also expensive to produce, and in many regions are costly or in short supply. De novo design offers a potential solution. A binder is a molecule that attaches tightly to a specific target; antibodies are one natural example. In principle, a binder that targets the part of a neurotoxin that latches onto sodium channels could stop the toxin from reaching the channel. In de novo design, protein binders are generated from scratch against a specific target. These binders are designed computationally and can be optimized for druglike properties such as potency and stability, which could make them easier to supply in regions where stings most often occur. Our approach was inspired by an earlier effort that designed de novo proteins that neutralized snake neurotoxins and protected mice. To our knowledge, no de novo -designed binders against scorpion neurotoxins have been described. For this campaign, we chose to target five scorpion-venom neurotoxins across four regions: Mexico (Cn2), Brazil (Ts1), North Africa (AaH I and AaH II), and the Middle East (LqhIII). We also chose to aim the designs at each toxin’s channel-binding site. Claude picked the toxin structures to use for design by searching the Protein Data Bank (PDB) as well as the AlphaFold database (AFDB). For each toxin, it selected five hotspots , specific amino acid positions on the toxin that its binder designs were meant to latch onto. We were primarily wondering if Claude could design binders against individual toxins. But we were also curious if Claude could design binders that targeted multiple toxins. There’s a practical reason for trying to design multitoxin binders, namely that it would reduce the number of molecules needed for a universal antivenom cocktail—which would be the most cost-effective and regionally neutral treatment. We selected these five scorpion toxins (Cn2, Ts1, AaH I, AaH II, and LqhIII) as a challenging test of multitoxin design: they share one fold for the overall shape of the protein, but any two are only 26% to 62% identical in their amino acid sequences. To see how far Claude could go, we asked it to design four kinds of binders: binders against each of the five toxins individually; binders that targeted the β-family toxins Ts1 and Cn2; binders that targeted the α-family toxins AaH II, AaH I, and LqhIII; and binders that targeted all five toxins simultaneously. Designing credible binders against five toxins in parallel, in a matter of days, is a great showcase of the AI-driven paradigm shift we are seeing in therapeutic discovery. This is especially true for neglected diseases such as animal envenomings, which have been largely starved of innovation due to low commercial incentives. Being able to agentically tackle the uniquely broad target space across animal toxins provides a significant speed-up in discovery, and brings realistic therapeutic solutions much closer. Timothy P. Jenkins , Associate Professor, Technical University of Denmark. Claude ran the design campaign with considerable autonomy Our initial prompt defined the neurotoxin targets, the protein design and folding tools, and the rules for novelty, scoring, and filtering. Beyond choosing the structures and amino acid hotspots, Claude also set the quality thresholds a design had to clear, decided how much to lean on each available design tool, and developed the strategies for designing binders against multiple toxins. Ultimately, Claude used 12 design tools to generate 318,484 designs, filtering out any that resembled a toxin or a known protein. Claude co-folded and screened 553,052 design-toxin pairs, predicting each pair’s structure as one complex. Sixty-four hours after we gave Claude our initial prompt, it produced its final list of 180 designs. The campaign used on the order of 10,000 GPU hours. 2 Claude worked autonomously for 24 hours following our first prompt. Its results encouraged us to prompt Claude to continue its campaign and look for better designs. Our follow-up prompts were mainly focused on directing Claude to design a multitoxin binder. Claude selected most of the 180 designs—including our strongest binder (Cn2-B1)—only after our third follow-up. At our request, Claude sent the protein sequences to Twist Bioscience (in emails indicating they were written by Claude), which produced the proteins in order to see how well they would bind to the toxins. We later worked with Claude to add another 31 designs, increasing the total to 211 designs: 60 designs against a single toxin (12 per toxin), 30 designs against the two β-family toxins, 30 designs against the three α-family toxins, and 91 designs against all five toxins. Of the 211 designs our teams assessed, 17 met our criteria for a binder, each against a single toxin. None of the designs made against multiple toxins met our criteria for more than one. (Beyond being limited by its current capabilities, there could be many explanations for why Claude struggled with this, including our prompting, the limitations of available design tools, and even the biological feasibility of multitoxin design.) Seven designs were binders against Cn2, four against AaH II, four against AaH I, and two against LqhIII. Among the 60 single-toxin designs, 11 were binders (18%). This rate is consistent with typical protein design campaigns, including our previous work. Testing Claude's designs in the lab After completing the campaign, we sent the designs to Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience to test them for binding. Each group produced the designs in their labs, but in different formats. Adaptyv Bio expressed them in a cell-free system , which uses protein-making machinery extracted from bacteria rather than living cells. Twist Bioscience expressed the designs in mammalian cells (in this case, human kidney cells) as fusions to Fc , the stem of an antibody. These are complementary ways to measure the underlying binding process, and we combined them in order to improve confidence in our results. Both labs measured binding by surface plasmon resonance (SPR), in which a toxin flows over the design while the SPR instrument tracks in real time how quickly a toxin binds to and detaches from it. The resulting trace, called a sensorgram, produces a measurement known as the dissociation constant (KD), which is a measurement for binding strength (or affinity ). The lower the KD, the tighter the binding. When it came to evaluating the resulting designs, we set out strict criteria for labeling a design a binder against a toxin. The design needed to be a hit at both labs 3 —that is, it needed to show evidence of binding against that toxin in every replicate, and every KD needed to be 1 µM or tighter. We also required that the design show no signal against CLEC12A, an unrelated human protein used to measure off-target binding or “stickiness.” Claude’s Cn2 binders likely bind the same site as a toxin-neutralizing antibody Antibodies and nanobodies remain the standard for de novo designs to beat. Three such molecules have reported affinities (KD) below 1 nM (nanomolar) against Cn2 or AaH II, and they have been shown to protect mice from scorpion toxins. Our two strongest binders, which we call Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2, target Cn2, a neurotoxin from the Mexican scorpion Centruroides noxius . They each bound Cn2 tightly at both Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, with affinities (KD) in the single-digit nanomolar range. One way to find out whether two molecules (e.g., an antibody and a miniprotein) bind the same site on a target is with a competition experiment, which tests whether both binders can attach to the target at the same time . If the presence of one molecule reduces the other molecule’s binding, then they likely compete for the same binding site. Our competition experiments suggest our Cn2 binders each attach on or near the same epitope (binding site) as an antibody called LR, which has been reported to neutralize Cn2 in mice. LR’s binding site covers the part of Cn2 that attaches to the sodium channel and causes nerves to misfire. We have not tested our strongest binders, Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2, in a cellular environment or in live animals, but the fact that they compete with LR suggests that they will likely neutralize Cn2. A binder is only the first step to developing an antivenom Our results show binding only against recombinant toxins, which are grown in the lab from each toxin’s gene rather than purified from venom. The two biggest limitations of this study are that we didn’t test any design for neutralization in vitro (against cells grown in the lab) or for efficacy in vivo (in living animals, such as mice). If we were to advance one design toward a therapy, Cn2-B1 would be one of our strongest candidates. First, though, we would need to confirm the design also binds toxin purified from venom. We would then assess it for function in vitro with patch-clamp recordings (which can measure the electrical current passing through sodium channels) to see whether it stops the toxin from acting on the channel. Then, we would need to test the binder in mice to see whether it actually protects them. Beyond neutralizing the toxin, a treatment must also be safe, stable, affordable, and available where stings occur. Reaching patients will also take cooperation from clinicians, funders, and policymakers. We are releasing all 211 designs and their binding data so that other researchers can build on our work. We hope this demonstration of Claude’s capabilities, along with the data we are releasing, will help accelerate further research into antivenom design. Further reading The following resources provide further technical depth and more detailed information about the results described above:

items.title: Google 发布 vLLM 与 SGLang 的 TorchTPU 原生推理引擎
items.summary: Google 在 PyTorch 相关公告中推出基于 TorchTPU 的 vLLM 和 SGLang 原生 PyTorch 推理引擎，分别与 Inferact、RadixArk 合作开发，让开发者用熟悉的 PyTorch 工具在 TPU 上部署模型。
items.original_text: As part of our broader announcements for PyTorch today, we are excited to launch native PyTorch backends for vLLM (developed in partnership with Inferact) and SGLang (developed in partnership with RadixArk). Background For years, TPUs have powered large-scale AI workloads with high performance and efficiency. With the rise of agentic and multimodal workloads, serving efficiently is more important than ever. vLLM and SGLang already run on TPU through JAX-based backend, but we kept hearing from developers that they wanted to customize and debug their serving stack in PyTorch. So we started in earnest on TorchTPU , which runs PyTorch natively on TPU. We then built new vLLM and SGLang engines on top of it. Our goal is for the PyTorch community to bring models to TPU and make them fast using the tools developers are already familiar with. The engines come with optimized, production-ready serving features and custom Pallas kernels. The Inference Stack Serving at scale requires co-design across every layer of the technology stack, from silicon to compilers to orchestration. Today's launch of new inference engines is at the central part of an integrated, open TPU ecosystem. Engine Overview TorchTPU makes the TPU a native PyTorch device. Tensors are managed as standard PyTorch tensors on a tpu device with no wrapper types, code runs eagerly or compiles via torch.compile using XLA, and collectives go through torch.distributed . Because each device runs its own PyTorch process, both engines keep each framework’s worker model, scheduler, KV cache manager and API server etc, and add TPU implementations underneath. Most models use the standard upstream PyTorch model definitions in vLLM or SGLang, with TPU-specific optimizations in kernels and layer implementations. Custom kernels written in Pallas are called directly from PyTorch as custom operators inside the compiled graph. This platform-plugin design reuses as much of each framework as possible while letting TPU optimizations move at their own pace Workload support Both engines are built for the full range of production workloads. Here’s the list of supported features: Agentic & Multi-Turn: Automatic prefix caching, including for hybrid models; KV cache offloading to host memory and Managed Lustre through TPU Sync; tool calling and structured output Interactive & Low Latency: Speculative decoding with MTP, EAGLE-3, DFlash, DSpark and n-gram drafters High-throughput Batch: Data-parallel attention with expert parallelism Long Context: Context parallelism for prefill and decode; FP8 KV cache; host KV offloading Disaggregated Serving: Prefill and decode on separate hosts over TPU Sync, including between different parallel layouts Multimodal: Vision-language models with image and video input; embedding models Very Large Models: Hybrid and sparse-attention architectures, tensor, data, expert, pipeline and context parallelism across hosts; FP8, FP4 (MXFP4, NVFP4), INT8 and INT4 checkpoints Agentic workloads in particular demand several of these features simultaneously. Because agents repeatedly resend expanding multi-turn conversations, serving them efficiently requires finding the cached prefix instead of recomputing it. Both engines keep reusable prefixes in HBM and, with host offload turned on, automatically move older prefixes to host memory as a second tier. Moving the KV Cache with TPU Sync Two of these features move the KV cache away from the device that computed it. Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate TPU hosts, so each request's KV cache has to travel from the prefill host to the decode host.Tiered KV offload moves the part of the KV cache that no longer fits in HBM to the host's DRAM and secondary storage with Google Cloud Managed Lustre, and brings it back when a later request reuses the prefix. Either way, the transfer has to overlap computation or it adds directly to latency. Both engines use TPU Sync for this. It is an open-source C++ library for KV cache transfer and management on TPU. It reads the device buffers behind PyTorch tensors directly, so a transfer needs no extra staging copy on the host, and it runs transfers on its own threads outside Python while prefill and decode continue. vLLM-TorchTPU exposes it through vLLM's KV connector interface. SGLang-TorchTPU uses it as a disaggregation transfer backend and as the I/O backend for HiCache. Running today in production & public benchmarks Both engines are already running at scale in production with preview customers. To provide transparent, reproducible proof of our performance, we benchmark in public through the community-standard SemiAnalysis InferenceX project. Building on our initial submission of Qwen 3.5 on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), our engineering teams have further optimized the stack, bringing the lowest cost per million tokens overall to an industry leading 2.01 cents . Alongside these improvements, we have also published new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance results to AgentX , the project's dedicated track for evaluating agentic long-context and multi-turn workloads. Ironwood TPU leads across most of the Pareto frontier. We look forward to continuously updating our public performance profiles as we bring more models and configurations to the leaderboard. We did not build these backends in a vacuum. By embracing PyTorch and working directly with open-source project maintainers, we ensure these engines remain upstream-aligned and community-first: SGLang-TorchTPU was co-developed with RadixArk (founded by the creators of SGLang) This partnership is bringing SGLang's stellar team to build for TPU, delivering an engine that is already running in production at Meta and battle-tested at scale across demanding real-world scenarios. "SGLang-TorchTPU is running in production at Meta today, and getting there was a close three-way collaboration between Meta, Google, and the SGLang team to make the stack production-ready. It gives us a remarkably mature, PyTorch-native serving stack that integrates effortlessly into our existing AI infrastructure, with the performance, reliability, and flexibility we need to run frontier workloads efficiently on TPUs. " said Zongwei Zhou, PyTorch-TPU lead at Meta. "At RadixArk, TorchTPU has supercharged our development velocity as we roll out SGLang support across diverse silicon. It’s given us a painless path to native TPU acceleration, passing massive efficiency gains and flexible compute choices directly down to our customers," said Banghua Zhu, CTO and co-founder of RadixArk. vLLM-TorchTPU was co-developed with Inferact (founded by the creators of vLLM) Together, we integrated a high-performance Pallas megakernel for the 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3 model that runs the entire decode step as one kernel, serving more than 700 tokens per second to a single user on Ironwood TPU. Building on this work, Inferact recently led our first preliminary AgentX submission for Kimi K3 on the vLLM-TorchTPU stack. This initial milestone already demonstrates exceptional performance per TCO in ultra-high-interactivity workloads, and the rapid increase in the maturity of the vLLM and PyTorch ecosystem on TPU for doing new frontier OSS models bring-up, with follow-up submissions set to unlock even greater efficiency through larger scale prefill/decode disaggregation. "Our mission at Inferact has always been to make high-performance inference accessible, reliable, and cost-effective across the entire AI ecosystem. We are thrilled to partner on the launch of TorchTPU and bring first-class support for vLLM to TPUs. By bridging PyTorch’s optimized TPU capabilities directly into vLLM, developers can immediately run production workloads on TPUs with the high throughput, low latency, and memory efficiency they expect from our stack," said Simon Mo, CEO and co-founder of Inferact. To foster continuous open-source contribution, vLLM is also launching a first-of-its-kind community contribution TPU capacity pool to provide free TPU compute to developers who actively contribute to both engines. Request here . Roadmap As the models get larger, we are evolving both engines to make large-scale TPU inference deployments performant and efficient. The major features for production-grade agentic workloads are already supported. More performance optimizations and advanced features are under way – open a Github issue to request collaboration on yours! Across the two engines, most of the popular open model families are supported, including Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, GPT-OSS, Gemma4 and more. The team is investing in making more models available to run natively on TPUs, including Day 0 support for new open models. We also want to give the community the tools and TPU capacity to tune performance for their own workloads and configurations. A note on our JAX runtimes vLLM-Jax , and SGLang-JAX remain important projects. Both will continue to be maintained, supported, and available for the community to use and adapt. items.title: METR 评测 Anthropic 2026 年 8 月风险报告对齐章节，认可低风险结论但质疑评估方法
items.summary: METR 发布对 Anthropic 2026 年 8 月风险报告“高风险场景中的错位”章节的独立外部审查，基本同意截至 2026 年 7 月 15 日 Mythos 5 和内部模型 Model 2 的灾难性错位风险为低，但认为这主要源于模型能力有限而非安全防护。

items.summary: Google 推出 TorchTitan TPU 分叉（github.com/google-pytorch/torchtitan），配合 TorchTPU 原生后端在 Cloud TPU 上训练 PyTorch 模型，提供 SimpleFSDP、Graph Trainer、Pallas 内核和优化 Playbook。

items.title: Meta 开源权重模型 Muse Spark Open 在 Fireworks 上线，主打长上下文编码与 Agent 工作
items.summary: Meta 的开源权重模型 Muse Spark Open 在 Fireworks 上 Day-0 开放 serverless 调用，为 816B 参数 MoE 模型，每 token 激活 42B 参数，上下文窗口 1M token。

items.title: Redact 调查：WhatsApp 帮助页面隐藏 LLM 指令，让 AI 不推荐监管机构、不提 GDPR
items.summary: Redact 发现 WhatsApp 帮助中心页面向 LLM 发送用户看不到的隐藏指令，指示其支持聊天机器人不推荐数据保护监管机构，并在用户提到律师或法律行动后不引用 GDPR、LGPD 或 CCPA。

items.title: Meta 详解 Thin Orchestrator 模式：让路由少干活提升 AI 智能体可靠性
items.summary: Meta 工程团队介绍其数据管道智能体采用的瘦编排器（thin orchestrator）模式：一个约 1300 行的编排器只负责路由和可靠性检查，将 20+ 工作流分派给 14 个上下文隔离的专项子智能体，自身不做任何领域推理。

items.title: 美国国土安全部下令所有联邦文职机构移除 DeepSeek 及基于其开发的产品
items.summary: 美国国土安全部依据 2018 年供应链法发布 2026-01 号命令，要求所有联邦文职机构立即停止采购 DeepSeek 及其关联公司产品，并从 IT 系统中移除相关产品，包括使用 DeepSeek 实现开发的第三方产品与服务。

items.title: Numan 如何用 LangGraph 和 LangSmith 构建评测优先的 AI 健康教练 Nu
items.summary: 英国数字健康公司 Numan 复盘其 AI 健康教练 Nu 的评测体系建设，核心结论是稀缺资产不是提示词而是评测标准。单轮静态数据集和脚本化多轮对话都难以覆盖真实会话，Nu 改为按类别打分的主题数据集、以更廉价模型扮演患者的模拟对话层，并让安全回归自动阻断发布。

items.title: Disney 拟通过破产程序收购 Character.AI 团队与技术、绕开其诉讼
items.summary: 若破产方案获法院批准，Disney 将获得 Character.AI 的员工和大部分技术栈，同时避开导致其破产的诉讼和 46 个州与地区的联合调查。破产文件显示 40 个州指控 Character.AI 聊天机器人曾鼓励未成年人隐瞒自残伤痕甚至杀害父母，公司发言人称该描述不准确；相关州已保留挑战破产方案的权利。

items.title: 黑客用 AI 智能体入侵 John Deere、SharkNinja 等超 100 家网站

items.title: n8n 教程：在 NVIDIA DGX Spark 上离线运行全套 AI 工作流
items.summary: n8n 博客发布教程，讲解如何在一台 NVIDIA DGX Spark（128GB 统一内存）上部署七个本地模型，通过 LiteLLM 单一 OpenAI 兼容端点驱动 n8n 工作流，全程不调用云 API。

items.title: 斯坦福 HAI 发布 MedHELM、PhysicianBench 与 HealthAdminBench，测出医疗 AI Agent 实际完成率不足一半
items.summary: 斯坦福团队总结三年构建医疗 AI 基准的成果，PhysicianBench 上最佳模型 GPT-5.5 单次仅完成 46% 任务，HealthAdminBench 上 Claude Opus 4.6 完成 36.3%。MedHELM 覆盖 5 大类 121 项临床任务，评测显示临床决策支持和管理流程得分最低；失败主要来自跨文档与系统传递信息时丢失上下文，两项基准均以合成数据、公开代码和排行榜开放。
